title: Finance for Executive Decision-Making
question: How should a leader decide where scarce money and talent go when every benefit is uncertain and every yes forecloses something else?

overview.text: Every leadership role eventually becomes a resource-allocation role. Whether you run a department, a hospital service line, a product team or a player development system, your most consequential decisions are about where money, people and time go — and what you give up by sending them there. This week builds the financial literacy to make those decisions rigorously and to hold your own finance partners, vendors and colleagues to the same standard.

The week moves from measurement to judgment. Lesson 1 shows how the three financial statements are built and why profit and cash can diverge sharply. Lesson 2 develops the time value of money — NPV, IRR, payback and the discount rate as an opportunity cost. Lesson 3 turns to cost behavior, marginal thinking, sunk and opportunity costs, and capital rationing. Lesson 4 confronts uncertainty: scenarios, expected value, real options and the systematic optimism of forecasts, including the live dispute over why big projects overrun. Lesson 5 applies everything to the economics of talent spending in sports organizations, where the value of a win is nonlinear and markets misprice skills until rivals catch up.

If you have studied economics, marginal analysis and opportunity cost will feel familiar; the emphasis here is executive: knowing which number answers which question, which assumption drives a result, and when a tidy calculation is hiding a judgment that belongs to the decision-makers. The Capital Allocation Lab lets you build a portfolio under a binding budget for a fictional hospital system. The case, The Budget Decision, puts a fictional club’s player development director between more people, better tools and deeper research capacity. The assignment asks you to write the kind of business case you would want to receive.

A note on evidence. Accounting and discounting are settled methods; the behavioral findings on sunk costs, opportunity-cost neglect and forecast optimism rest on experiments and field studies of varying strength; and two of this week’s most interesting claims — why large projects overrun, and whether top draft picks are overpriced — are actively disputed. You will see both sides.

objectives: Read and link the three financial statements, and diagnose gaps between accrual profit and operating cash flow.
Compute and interpret NPV, IRR, payback and a weighted average cost of capital, and choose the right rule for mutually exclusive and capital-rationed decisions.
Separate relevant from sunk and allocated costs, price opportunity cost explicitly, and reason at the margin.
Evaluate investments under uncertainty with sensitivity and scenario analysis, real-options reasoning and reference-class forecasting.
Value talent spending as surplus over cost against an explicit objective, and judge evidence about mispricing in talent markets.
Write a financial justification that a skeptical decision-maker can audit.

lessons.title: Three Statements, One Story: Profit, Cash and Position
lessons.summary: How the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement are built on accrual accounting, how they link, and why profit and cash can diverge sharply.
objectives: Explain what each of the three financial statements measures and how accrual accounting differs from cash accounting.
Trace how net income, depreciation, working capital and capital spending connect the three statements.
Reconcile profit to operating cash flow for a simple organization and diagnose why they differ.
Translate a departmental proposal into its effects on reported expense, cash and the balance sheet.
lessons.executive: Profit and cash answer different questions. The income statement measures performance on an accrual basis — revenue when earned, costs matched to the period — so a growing organization can report healthy profit while cash drains into unpaid customer invoices and new equipment. The balance sheet records what the organization owns and owes at a moment; the cash flow statement reconciles the two. For decisions, insist on seeing all three, ask what drives any gap between profit and operating cash flow, and know whether a proposal will be treated as an operating expense or a capital asset, because that choice changes how its cost appears without changing what it costs.

explore.text: Imagine a company whose income statement shows record profit in the same quarter it struggles to make payroll. Nothing fraudulent has happened. Its customers simply pay sixty days after they are invoiced, its sales doubled, and it bought new equipment for cash. The accountants are right that the company earned money; the treasurer is right that the company is short of it. Both are describing the same organization through different lenses.

Executives who are not finance specialists often treat “the numbers” as one thing. They are at least three things, each answering a different question, and many expensive misunderstandings in budget meetings come from mixing them up: a proposal that “pays for itself” on a profit view may consume cash for years, and a cost-cutting move that improves this year’s cash may quietly create a liability on the balance sheet.

Before reading on: a software firm books $10 million of revenue and reports $2.25 million of net income in its first year. Could its cash flow from operations be close to zero? Write down two things that would have to be true.

Hypothetical illustration from healthcare: a physician group expands into a new specialty, bills insurers for every visit and records the revenue immediately. Insurers pay weeks or months later, and some claims are denied and must be resubmitted. On the income statement the expansion succeeds in its first quarter; in the bank account it looks like a loss until collections catch up. If the group’s leaders read only one of these views, they will draw the wrong conclusion about whether to keep expanding.

understand.text: Three statements, three questions

The **income statement** reports performance over a period: revenues minus expenses equals net income. The **balance sheet** reports position at a moment: what the organization owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the residual belonging to owners (equity), with assets always equal to liabilities plus equity. The **statement of cash flows** reports where cash came from and went during the period, split into operating, investing and financing activities. Standard introductory texts build all three from the same transactions.

The income statement is prepared on an **accrual basis**. Revenue is recognized when it is earned — when the service is delivered or the goods change hands — not when cash arrives, and expenses are matched to the period whose revenue they helped produce. Cash accounting, by contrast, records only receipts and payments. Accrual accounting gives a better picture of performance; it also creates the gap between profit and cash that this lesson is about.

understand.caption: How the three statements link (indirect method)

steps.label: Income statement
steps.text: Revenue − expenses (including non-cash depreciation) = net income.

steps.label: Equity
steps.text: Net income not paid out increases retained earnings on the balance sheet.

steps.label: Operating cash flow
steps.text: Start from net income; add back non-cash expenses; subtract increases in receivables and inventory; add increases in payables.

steps.label: Investing and financing
steps.text: Subtract purchases of long-lived assets; add money raised from owners or lenders; subtract repayments and distributions.

steps.label: Balance sheet cash
steps.text: Beginning cash + total change in cash = ending cash, which must equal cash on the balance sheet.

understand.text: Work through a synthetic example. Kestrelwick Software (fictional) begins with no cash. Its founders invest $2.5 million. In year one it sells $10.0 million of subscriptions on credit and collects $7.0 million, leaving $3.0 million in accounts receivable. It pays $5.0 million of salaries. Its hosting bill is $1.5 million, of which $1.2 million is paid and $0.3 million is still owed at year end. On the first day it buys $2.0 million of equipment, expected to last four years, so straight-line depreciation is $0.5 million a year. Income tax at 25% is paid in cash.

understand.caption: Kestrelwick Software, year one (in $ thousands)
understand.note: Synthetic data. Assumptions: all sales on credit; tax paid in cash; no interest, inventory or distributions.

understand.text: Net income is $2.25 million; cash from operations is $50 thousand. The $2.2 million gap has a precise anatomy: $3.0 million of revenue was earned but not yet collected (it sits in receivables), offset by $0.5 million of depreciation that reduced profit without using cash this year and $0.3 million of hosting cost that was expensed but not yet paid. You can confirm the operating figure directly: collections of $7.0 million minus cash paid for salaries ($5.0 million), hosting ($1.2 million) and tax ($0.75 million) equals $0.05 million. The direct and indirect methods must agree; if they do not, something has been misclassified.

understand.caption: Kestrelwick balance sheet at the end of year one (in $ thousands)
understand.note: Synthetic data, continuing the example above.

understand.text: The balance sheet closes the loop. Ending cash of $550 thousand matches the cash flow statement. Retained earnings equal the year’s net income because nothing was distributed. Equipment appears at cost less accumulated depreciation, which is why buying it did not hit the income statement all at once: the $2.0 million left the bank on day one, but only $0.5 million was recognized as expense this year. Every one of the statement links in the flow diagram is visible in these three small tables.

understand.title: Prerequisite: the accounting equation and the vocabulary

blocks.text: The accounting equation — assets equal liabilities plus equity — holds after every transaction, because each transaction changes at least two accounts. Selling on credit raises an asset (receivables) and raises equity through revenue. Paying a supplier lowers an asset (cash) and lowers a liability (payables).

items: **Working capital** is current assets minus current liabilities. Changes in receivables, inventory and payables are the usual reasons operating cash flow differs from profit.
**Depreciation** spreads the cost of a long-lived asset over its useful life. It is an expense without a cash payment in that period; the cash left when the asset was bought.

**Capital expenditure (capex)** is spending on long-lived assets; it appears in investing cash flows and on the balance sheet. **Operating expense (opex)** is consumed in the period and appears on the income statement immediately.
**Retained earnings** accumulate net income that has not been distributed to owners.

challenge.text: Statements are disciplined, not neutral. Every figure rests on estimates and conventions: how long equipment will last, how much of the receivables will never be collected, when a multi-year contract’s revenue counts as earned. Two well-run organizations with identical economics can report different profits because they made different, defensible estimates. When a number surprises you, ask which estimate drives it before asking whether the business changed.

The statements also omit much of what matters most in knowledge-intensive organizations. Spending on people, training and research is largely expensed as it occurs (some software development costs can be capitalized under specific rules), so an organization’s most valuable capabilities — a trained staff, a proprietary model, a reputation with recruits — usually do not appear as assets at all. A department that invests heavily in developing people looks costly on the income statement and asset-light on the balance sheet. That is an accounting convention, not evidence that the investment has no value, and it is one reason finance offices and operating leaders talk past each other.

Neither profit nor cash is “the truth.” Cash can be flattered for a quarter by delaying payments to suppliers or cutting maintenance; profit can be flattered by optimistic estimates. Each is harder to manipulate when read alongside the other two statements. The useful habit is triangulation: when profit rises and operating cash flow falls for several periods, find the working-capital or estimation story that explains it.

challenge.title: Methodological note: free cash flow, EBITDA and “adjusted” numbers

blocks.text: **Free cash flow** is commonly defined as cash from operations minus capital expenditure: the cash available to repay lenders or return to owners after keeping the asset base going. For Kestrelwick it is $50 thousand minus $2.0 million, or −$1.95 million — a growth company consuming cash, which is normal, provided someone is willing to finance it.

**EBITDA** (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) is popular because it approximates operating cash generation before investment. It ignores two things that consume cash: capital spending and growth in working capital. For Kestrelwick, EBITDA is $3.5 million while operating cash flow is $50 thousand. Any “adjusted” earnings measure deserves the same treatment: find the reconciliation to the standard figure and read each adjustment as a claim that must be justified.

apply.text: Hypothetical illustration from a hospital: a revenue-cycle backlog lets receivables grow by several weeks of billings. The income statement is unchanged, but cash tightens and the finance office proposes a hiring freeze. The real problem is collection, not profitability; a leader who reads only the profit line will cut the wrong thing.

Hypothetical illustration from a law firm: many professional partnerships manage closely on cash, while their accrual books show substantial unbilled work and uncollected invoices. A partner who records a strong year of billed hours may still see a small distribution if clients pay slowly. Asking “earned or collected?” resolves most of these disputes quickly.

Hypothetical illustration from government: agencies often budget on a cash or obligation basis. Deferring maintenance improves this year’s budget position while creating a larger repair bill later — a liability that a cash budget does not show. Accrual thinking asks what obligations a decision creates, not only what it spends this year.

apply.title: Executive twist: “It is accretive to earnings”

blocks.text: A finance partner tells you a proposed acquisition of a small analytics vendor is “accretive to earnings in year one.” You have ten minutes before the decision meeting. The claim may be true and still incomplete. Ask four questions: What is the cash profile for the first three years, including integration costs? What new liabilities come with it (contracts, retention bonuses, lease obligations)? Which estimates make year-one earnings look good — for example, a long amortization period for what was bought? And what would the same money earn in its next-best use? You will not resolve all four in ten minutes, but asking them changes what the meeting decides.

apply.text: Professional application in baseball operations: suppose a player development department proposes a $750,000 data platform. If the club buys and capitalizes it, cash leaves at once but this year’s operating budget may show only one year of depreciation; if it is licensed as a subscription with similar total cost, the full annual fee hits the operating budget every year. Neither treatment changes the economics, but they change how the proposal looks in the budget review and which approval track it follows. The same logic applies to any large upfront payment that finance may spread over several years for reporting: ask early how it will be treated, and present both the cash profile and the reported-expense profile so no one is surprised later.

items: What does each statement say, and do they tell the same story about this period?
Where is operating cash flow diverging from profit, and which working-capital line explains it?
Which estimates (useful lives, collectability, revenue timing) most affect the reported result?
What obligations does this decision create that will not appear in this year’s budget?
Is the proposal being judged as capex or opex, and is that treatment shaping the debate?

retain.text: The income statement measures accrual performance over a period, the balance sheet measures position at a moment, and the cash flow statement reconciles profit to the change in cash. Profit and cash diverge through non-cash expenses, working capital and capital spending; every divergence has an anatomy you can trace. Read the three together, and know how your own proposals will be classified.
Without looking back: list the three adjustments that took Kestrelwick from $2.25 million of net income to $50 thousand of operating cash flow.
Name one decision in your current work whose cash profile and reported-expense profile differ. Which one does your organization’s approval process actually look at?
Why can a fast-growing organization be profitable and short of cash at the same time?

takeaways: Each statement answers a different question: performance (income statement), position (balance sheet), and cash movement (cash flow statement).
Accrual profit and operating cash flow diverge through depreciation, working capital and capital spending — trace the anatomy of any gap.
The statements omit most investments in people and capability, which are expensed as incurred.
Capex versus opex treatment changes how a proposal looks in a budget review without changing its economics; present both profiles.

check.prompt: A company reports net income of $4.0 million and depreciation of $1.2 million. During the year, accounts receivable increased by $2.5 million, inventory decreased by $0.4 million and accounts payable increased by $0.6 million. What is its cash flow from operations, in $ millions (indirect method)?
check.working: Start with net income: 4.0. Add back non-cash depreciation: 4.0 + 1.2 = 5.2. Subtract the increase in receivables (revenue earned but not collected): 5.2 − 2.5 = 2.7. Add the decrease in inventory (stock sold that was paid for earlier): 2.7 + 0.4 = 3.1. Add the increase in payables (expenses not yet paid): 3.1 + 0.6 = 3.7.
check.explanation: Operating cash flow equals net income plus non-cash expenses, minus increases in operating assets (receivables, inventory) and plus increases in operating liabilities (payables). Here that is 4.0 + 1.2 − 2.5 + 0.4 + 0.6 = $3.7 million. The signs follow cash logic: an asset that grew absorbed cash; a liability that grew is cash you have not yet paid out.

check.prompt: Which event would raise this year’s reported net income while lowering this year’s cash from operations?

options.text: Paying a supplier invoice that was already recorded as an expense last year.
A large increase in sales made on 90-day credit terms, with costs paid in cash.
Buying a new server rack for cash at year end.
Raising money from a bank loan.

check.explanation: Credit sales are recognized as revenue when earned, raising profit, but the cash has not arrived while the costs of serving those customers were paid. Receivables rise, which absorbs operating cash. This is the classic growth-driven gap between profit and cash.

optionFeedback.a: Paying an old, already-expensed invoice lowers cash but does not change this year’s income — no profit effect.
optionFeedback.c: A capital purchase lowers cash through investing activities and does not raise net income; depreciation will reduce income later.
optionFeedback.d: A loan raises cash through financing activities and has no effect on net income (until interest is charged).

check.prompt: A department buys $900,000 of equipment with a three-year useful life (straight-line, no salvage value) on the first day of the year. What is the effect on this year’s income statement and cash flow statement?

options.text: Expense of $900,000 on the income statement; investing outflow of $900,000.
Depreciation expense of $300,000; investing outflow of $900,000.
Depreciation expense of $300,000; operating outflow of $300,000.
No income statement effect until the equipment is sold; financing outflow of $900,000.

check.explanation: Capitalized equipment is expensed through depreciation over its useful life — $900,000 ÷ 3 = $300,000 this year — while the full cash payment appears as an investing outflow when the purchase is made. On the indirect cash flow statement, the $300,000 of depreciation is added back to net income because it used no cash this year.

optionFeedback.a: Expensing the whole cost immediately is what happens to an operating expense, not a capitalized asset.
optionFeedback.c: Depreciation is a non-cash expense; the cash left in full, as an investing outflow, when the equipment was bought.
optionFeedback.d: Depreciation begins when the asset is placed in service, and buying equipment is an investing, not financing, activity.

lessons.title: The Price of Time: NPV, IRR, Payback and the Cost of Capital
lessons.summary: Discounting turns cash flows at different dates into comparable values; NPV is the decision rule, IRR and payback are summaries with known traps, and the discount rate is an opportunity cost.
objectives: Compute present values, NPV, IRR and simple and discounted payback for a short cash-flow series.
Explain why the discount rate is an opportunity cost and how a weighted average cost of capital is built.
Identify when IRR and payback mislead — scale, timing, non-conventional cash flows — and choose the right rule.
Diagnose the common practice of applying one firm-wide rate to projects of different risk.
lessons.executive: A dollar later is worth less than a dollar now because money now can be invested. Net present value converts every future cash flow into today’s dollars at the return you could earn elsewhere at similar risk, then subtracts the cost: positive NPV means the project beats its alternative. IRR and payback are useful summaries, but IRR favors small, quick projects and can be ambiguous, and payback ignores everything after the break-even date. Use NPV to decide, report IRR and payback as context, and insist that riskier projects face a higher discount rate rather than a single company-wide hurdle.

explore.text: A city offers a contractor a choice in settling a claim: $1.0 million today or $1.3 million in four years, guaranteed. Most people’s instinct is to compare the two numbers. The right comparison is between $1.0 million today and what $1.3 million in four years is worth today — and that depends entirely on what the money could earn in the meantime.
Before reading on: at what annual return would you be indifferent between the two offers? Make a guess, then check it against the calculation below.

If the contractor can earn 6% a year at similar risk, $1.3 million in four years is worth $1.3 million ÷ 1.06⁴ ≈ $1,029,722 today, so waiting is better. At 8% it is worth $1.3 million ÷ 1.08⁴ ≈ $955,539, so taking the money now is better. The indifference rate is the return at which $1.0 million grows to exactly $1.3 million in four years: 1.3^(1/4) − 1 ≈ 6.78%. Same cash, different decision, depending on a single number that nobody wrote on the offer — the opportunity cost of waiting.

Hypothetical illustration from pharmaceuticals and energy: projects whose payoffs arrive ten or twenty years out are extraordinarily sensitive to this number. Raising the rate from 6% to 10% cuts the present value of a dollar received in year fifteen from about 42 cents to about 24 cents. Many disagreements about “long-term thinking” are, underneath, disagreements about the discount rate.

understand.text: Discounting and net present value

The present value of a cash flow C received in t years at rate r is C ÷ (1 + r)ᵗ. **Net present value** sums the present values of all a project’s cash flows, including the negative initial outlay. A positive NPV means the project returns more than the rate used to discount it, so accepting it adds value relative to the alternative; a negative NPV means the alternative is better. Introductory finance texts present NPV as the primary capital-budgeting rule for this reason.

The **internal rate of return** is the discount rate at which NPV equals zero — the project’s own break-even return. The **payback period** is the time until cumulative cash inflows recover the initial outlay; **discounted payback** does the same with discounted cash flows. The **profitability index** divides the present value of future cash flows by the initial outlay and is most useful when capital is scarce.

understand.caption: Two projects, each costing $1,000 (in $ thousands), discounted at 8%
understand.note: Synthetic data. Payback interpolates within the year in which cumulative cash turns positive.

understand.text: The table is a small lesson in itself. Quick has the higher IRR and recovers its cost in a year and a half; Long has the higher NPV and profitability index. If the two are mutually exclusive — say, two designs for the same system — the rules disagree. NPV says choose Long: at an 8% cost of capital, it adds about $98 thousand more value. IRR favors Quick because it returns cash early, and early cash is worth more when rates are high. The two NPV profiles cross at about 13.6%: below that rate Long is better, above it Quick is better. So the disagreement is not a paradox; it tells you the choice depends on the discount rate, which is exactly the number you should be debating.
The discount rate is an opportunity cost

The discount rate is not an accounting entry; it is the return investors could earn elsewhere on investments of similar risk. For a whole firm, that is often approximated by the **weighted average cost of capital (WACC)**: the after-tax cost of debt and the cost of equity, each weighted by its share of financing. With 60% equity costing 11%, 40% debt costing 6% and a 25% tax rate, WACC = 0.60 × 11% + 0.40 × 6% × (1 − 0.25) = 6.6% + 1.8% = 8.4%. The cost of equity is not observed directly; it is usually estimated from a model such as the capital asset pricing model.

Practice departs from theory in instructive ways. In Graham and Harvey’s survey of 392 chief financial officers, large firms relied heavily on present-value techniques and the capital asset pricing model, smaller firms were relatively more likely to use payback, and a surprising number of firms used a firm-wide discount rate rather than one matched to each project’s risk. A single company rate overvalues risky projects and undervalues safe ones, so over time it steers capital toward risk.

understand.title: Prerequisite: compounding and discounting by hand

blocks.text: Compounding moves money forward: $1,000 invested at 8% grows to 1,000 × 1.08 = $1,080 after one year and 1,000 × 1.08³ ≈ $1,259.71 after three. Discounting moves money backward by dividing by the same factor: $1,000 received in three years is worth 1,000 ÷ 1.259712 ≈ $793.83 today at 8%. Every NPV is just this operation repeated for each year and summed.

Two shortcuts save time. An **annuity** of C per year for n years is worth C × [1 − (1 + r)⁻ⁿ] ÷ r today; at 8% for five years the factor is about 3.9927, so $100 a year is worth about $399.27. A **perpetuity** of C per year forever is worth C ÷ r — $100 a year at 8% is worth $1,250 — and if it grows at rate g it is worth C ÷ (r − g), or $2,000 at 8% with 3% growth. The growing-perpetuity formula explodes as g approaches r, which is why terminal values in valuations deserve suspicion.

items: **Scale.** IRR is a percentage, so it ignores size. Compare two one-year projects at a 9% cost of capital: $50,000 returning 40% adds about $14,000 of NPV (70,000 ÷ 1.09 − 50,000), while $5 million returning 15% adds about $275,000 (5.75 million ÷ 1.09 − 5 million). When projects compete for the same slot, compare NPVs.

**Timing.** Between mutually exclusive projects, IRR favors early cash, as Quick versus Long showed. Textbooks often describe this as an implicit assumption that interim cash is reinvested at the IRR; whatever the framing, the practical rule is to compare NPVs or compute the IRR of the incremental cash flows (Long minus Quick), which is about 13.6% here and should be compared with the cost of capital.

**Non-conventional cash flows.** When the sign of the cash flows changes more than once, there can be several IRRs or none. A project with flows of −100, +230 and −132 (a cleanup cost at the end) has IRRs of both 10% and 20%; its NPV is positive only for discount rates between them. Reporting “the IRR” of such a project is meaningless.

**Payback’s blind spots.** Payback ignores the time value of money and everything after the cutoff. A project that breaks even in two years and then stops is ranked above one that breaks even in three years and pays for ten.

challenge.text: Payback survives in practice for reasons worth respecting. It is easy to explain, it is a rough guard against liquidity strain, and distant cash flows are usually the least reliable part of any forecast. But truncating the forecast is a crude way to express distrust. If you doubt year-seven benefits, say so explicitly — lower them, widen the scenario range or test the break-even — rather than pretending they are zero.

Two further cautions. First, avoid double-counting risk: managers who both shade the cash flows down for risk and raise the discount rate for the same risk penalize the project twice. Choose one place to adjust and document it. Second, inflation must be handled consistently: discount nominal cash flows (which include expected price increases) at a nominal rate, or real cash flows at a real rate. Mixing them is an easy and consequential error in departmental business cases.

challenge.title: Methodological note: where discount rates come from

blocks.text: In corporate finance the cost of equity is commonly estimated with the capital asset pricing model: the risk-free rate plus the asset’s sensitivity to market movements (beta) times the market risk premium. The cost of debt is the yield the organization pays to borrow, reduced by the tax deductibility of interest. WACC combines the two. Each input is an estimate, so a plausible range for WACC is often a percentage point or two wide. Survey evidence indicates that large firms rely heavily on the capital asset pricing model in practice.

Inside organizations, a published “hurdle rate” is frequently set above the estimated cost of capital. Defenders say this compensates for optimistic forecasts or rations scarce capital; critics say it hides two separate judgments inside one number. Public bodies face a different debate: whether to discount at the government’s borrowing rate, a social rate reflecting how society trades present for future welfare, or something else. You do not need to settle these debates to lead well, but you should know which one your finance office has settled and why.

apply.text: Hypothetical illustration from local government: a city compares an LED streetlight retrofit with a road resurfacing program. The retrofit saves a modest amount every year for twenty years; resurfacing avoids a large repair bill in year three. At a low discount rate the retrofit wins; at a high rate resurfacing wins. A council that argues about “sustainability versus potholes” is really arguing about the discount rate and the reliability of twenty-year savings estimates — and can resolve the argument faster by debating those directly.

Hypothetical illustration from consulting and technology: a firm considering a three-year client-analytics platform sees an IRR of 35% in the vendor’s deck. On inspection the initial outlay excludes internal staff time and the benefits start in month one. Rebuilding the cash flows with integration costs and a six-month ramp lowers the IRR to the low teens — still positive NPV at the firm’s cost of capital, but no longer the obvious winner over a cheaper process change.

apply.title: Executive twist: one hurdle rate for every department

blocks.text: Your organization evaluates every proposal at a 10% hurdle rate. A low-risk energy retrofit with dependable savings is rejected at 10% but would be accepted at the 6% that matches its risk; a speculative new venture clears 10% on optimistic numbers. Over several years, the single rate quietly shifts the portfolio toward risk. You cannot rebuild the finance function, but you can ask, in each review, two questions: is this project riskier or safer than our average investment, and does its rate reflect that? Proposing two or three risk tiers is usually an easier sell than a full project-by-project rate.

apply.text: Professional application in baseball operations: compensation terms are a time-value problem. Consider two fictional contract structures with the same $50 million nominal total: $10 million a year for five years, or $6 million a year for five years plus $20 million deferred to year ten. At a 6% discount rate the first is worth about $42.12 million today; the second is worth about $25.27 million plus $11.17 million, or $36.44 million — roughly $5.7 million less in present value for the payer, despite identical headline totals. The same arithmetic applies to multi-year staff contracts, facility leases and vendor agreements. When anyone reports a total, ask for the present value and the rate used.

A practical routine for any investment memo: lay out the cash flows year by year (not accounting profit), state the discount rate and why it fits the project’s risk, report NPV first, then IRR and payback as context, and show how NPV changes if the rate moves two points in either direction. If the decision flips within that range, the rate is the issue to discuss.

retain.text: Money has a time value because it has alternative uses. NPV discounts cash flows at the return available on comparable-risk alternatives and is the rule to decide by. IRR and payback are summaries that mislead on scale, timing and unusual cash-flow patterns. The discount rate is an opportunity cost that should rise with risk; a single company-wide rate distorts choices.

Use NPV to choose between mutually exclusive projects; IRR favors small and early-paying projects and can be ambiguous.
Payback ignores time value and post-payback cash; treat it as a liquidity screen, not a decision rule.
The discount rate should match the project’s risk; a single firm-wide rate steers capital toward riskier projects.

check.prompt: A project costs $500 today and returns $200 at the end of year 1, $250 at the end of year 2 and $200 at the end of year 3. What is its NPV at a 10% discount rate? Give the answer in dollars to the nearest dollar.
check.explanation: NPV is the sum of each cash flow divided by (1 + r) raised to its year, including the outlay at year 0. The inflows are worth $538.69 today at 10%, so the project adds about $38.69 of value relative to the 10% alternative.

check.prompt: Two mutually exclusive projects have the same cost. Project A has an IRR of 22% and an NPV of $140,000 at the 9% cost of capital; Project B has an IRR of 16% and an NPV of $210,000. Which should you choose, and why?

options.text: A, because a higher IRR means a better return on every dollar invested.
B, because it adds more value at the organization’s actual cost of capital.
Either: the rules conflict, so the choice is arbitrary.
A, because projects with higher IRRs are always less risky.

check.explanation: For mutually exclusive projects, NPV at the appropriate cost of capital is the decision rule: B adds $70,000 more value. A’s higher IRR typically reflects earlier cash flows, which IRR rewards; that advantage only dominates if the relevant discount rate is above the crossover rate of the two NPV profiles.

optionFeedback.a: IRR is a rate, not an amount of value, and it implicitly favors early cash; it can rank mutually exclusive projects incorrectly.
optionFeedback.c: The conflict is resolvable: NPV at the right rate decides, or equivalently the IRR of the incremental cash flows compared with the cost of capital.
optionFeedback.d: IRR says nothing directly about risk; risk belongs in the discount rate or the cash-flow scenarios.

check.prompt: A firm’s capital is 70% equity costing 12% and 30% debt costing 5% before tax, with a 25% tax rate. Which is its weighted average cost of capital, and when is it the right discount rate?

options.text: 9.525%, appropriate for projects whose risk resembles the firm’s average.
9.9%, appropriate for every project the firm evaluates.
8.5%, appropriate for projects safer than the firm’s average.
9.525%, appropriate for every project, because it is the firm’s cost of money.

check.explanation: WACC = 0.70 × 12% + 0.30 × 5% × (1 − 0.25) = 8.4% + 1.125% = 9.525%. It is the right rate for projects with the firm’s average risk; safer projects deserve a lower rate and riskier ones a higher rate.

optionFeedback.b: 9.9% ignores the tax deductibility of interest (it uses 5% instead of 3.75%), and no single rate is right for every project.
optionFeedback.c: 8.5% is not the weighted average implied by these inputs.
optionFeedback.d: The arithmetic is right, but applying one rate to all projects regardless of risk is the error documented in practice.

lessons.title: Thinking at the Margin: Cost Behavior, Unit Economics and Capital Rationing
lessons.summary: Decisions turn on incremental, future, avoidable costs and benefits — not averages, allocations or sunk costs — and when money is scarce, on value per constrained dollar.
objectives: Classify costs as fixed, variable or step-fixed and compute contribution margin and break-even volume.
Separate relevant (incremental, avoidable, future) costs from sunk and allocated costs in a decision.
Price opportunity cost explicitly, including the cost of scarce staff time.
Choose a portfolio under a binding budget using NPV per dollar and enumeration of combinations.
lessons.executive: Averages describe the past; margins decide the future. The question for any decision is what changes if you say yes: which costs and benefits are incremental, avoidable and still ahead of you. Costs already incurred are sunk and irrelevant except for any salvage value; allocated overhead often does not move at all. Every yes also consumes something scarce — money, staff hours, leadership attention — so the true cost includes the best alternative use of it, which people routinely neglect unless it is named. When the budget binds, rank projects by value per scarce dollar and check combinations, because the best set is not always the best individual projects.

explore.text: Hypothetical illustration from an airline: a 180-seat flight leaves in two hours with twenty empty seats. The finance team’s report says the average cost per seat on this route is about $180. A last-minute buyer offers $79. Selling below average cost sounds like a loss. But almost all of the flight’s cost — aircraft, crew, most of the fuel, airport fees — is already committed whether the seat is filled or not. The extra cost of carrying one more passenger is small: a little fuel, a snack, a booking fee. If that marginal cost is $25, the sale adds $54 to the flight’s result, provided it does not teach full-fare customers to wait for bargains.

Before reading on: list three costs in your organization that are reported as an “average per unit” (per player, per patient, per case, per user). For each, is the average a good guide to the cost of one more unit?

The airline case contains the three ideas of this lesson. First, costs behave differently as activity changes, and averages hide that behavior. Second, the only costs that belong in a decision are those that differ between the options and have not yet been incurred. Third, every choice uses something that could have been used elsewhere — here, a seat that might have gone to a later, higher-paying buyer — and that forgone alternative is a real cost even though no invoice records it.

understand.text: Cost behavior and contribution margin

**Variable costs** rise in proportion to activity (supplies per procedure, transaction fees per order). **Fixed costs** do not change within a relevant range and time horizon (rent, a salaried team, a software license). **Step-fixed costs** are fixed over a range and then jump (one supervisor per twelve staff). Whether a cost is fixed depends on the horizon: over a quarter, most salaries are fixed; over three years, almost everything is variable because you can choose not to renew.

**Contribution margin** is price minus variable cost per unit: what each additional unit contributes toward covering fixed costs and then profit. **Break-even volume** is fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit. These two numbers answer most “should we add this?” questions faster than any full income statement.

understand.caption: Worked example: adding an evening imaging shift at a hospital (monthly)
rows: Variable cost per scan (supplies, per-scan fees)
Fixed cost of opening the shift (staff, utilities)

understand.text: The table also shows why break-even analysis is a risk tool. The shift is profitable at expected volume, but a cushion of 40 scans over break-even is only a 25% margin of safety, and a $50 cut in average reimbursement raises the break-even point by 30 scans. Before approving, a leader should ask how confident the volume forecast is and what in the contract environment could move the price.
Relevant costs, sunk costs and opportunity costs

understand.caption: Is this cost relevant to the decision?
cells: Irrelevant to the choice, though it still belongs in the budget.
The past payment is irrelevant; only its salvage or reuse value, which can differ between options, counts.
Relevant: the only costs that belong in the comparison.
understand.note: Original teaching device. Only costs that are not yet incurred and differ between options belong in the comparison; a past purchase matters only through its salvage or reuse value.

understand.text: The **sunk-cost effect** is the tendency to continue an endeavor because money, time or effort has already been invested. In Arkes and Blumer’s classic studies, people faced with a nearly finished but now unpromising project — the best-known scenario involves an airline president and a research project — tended to keep investing; those with a sunk cost also rated the project’s chances of success as higher, prior courses in economics did not reduce the effect, and the authors connect it to a wish not to appear wasteful.

**Opportunity cost** is the value of the best alternative forgone. It is invisible in accounting records, and experiments suggest people often ignore it unless prompted. In studies by Frederick and colleagues, simply reminding buyers that money not spent could be used for other purchases reduced purchase rates and shifted choices toward cheaper options, and the authors argue that greater effort alone does not usually overcome the neglect. The organizational implication is procedural: alternatives that are not written into the proposal are rarely weighed.

**Marginal analysis** combines these ideas: keep adding an activity while the incremental benefit of the next unit exceeds its incremental cost, including opportunity cost. The second analyst on a project may add more than the first; the fifth may add less than she would elsewhere. The right question is never “is this team valuable?” but “what does one more (or one fewer) unit of this change?”

blocks.text: Suppose a tutoring program costs $90,000 a year in fixed staff costs plus $200 per student in materials. With 300 students, the average cost is 90,000 ÷ 300 + 200 = $500 per student. The marginal cost of the 301st student is $200 — the materials — as long as the staff can absorb one more. If the program is at capacity and the 301st student requires a new tutor, the marginal cost of that student jumps to the tutor’s full cost. Average cost is a fact about the past mix; marginal cost depends on where you are relative to capacity.

understand.text: Capital rationing: when good projects compete for scarce money

If an organization could raise unlimited money at its cost of capital, it would accept every positive-NPV project. Inside a club, hospital or agency, budgets are fixed by policy, so capital is rationed. Then the question becomes which set of projects creates the most total NPV within the budget. For divisible projects, rank by the **profitability index** (present value of future cash flows ÷ initial cost, equivalently NPV per dollar plus one) and fund down the list. For indivisible projects, ranking can fail; check the feasible combinations.

understand.caption: Capital rationing with a $1,000 budget (in $ thousands)
rows: Found by checking every feasible set
understand.note: Synthetic data. All four projects have positive NPV; the budget allows only some.

understand.text: Ranking by profitability index picks P2 and P3 for $300 thousand of NPV and strands $100 thousand that no remaining project can use. Checking combinations finds P1 and P2, which spend the whole budget for $320 thousand. The difference is the opportunity cost of using a rule of thumb. Note also what rationing implies about value: under a binding budget, each project’s real cost is not just its price but the NPV of whatever it displaces.

challenge.text: Sunk-cost reasoning is not always an error. Past investment can carry information — a team that has spent two years learning a system may now be able to finish it cheaply, which is a lower remaining cost, not a sunk-cost argument. Honoring a commitment can protect reputation with partners and recruits. Abandoning projects at the first setback can teach staff that no initiative will be supported long enough to work. The discipline is to translate each of these into forward-looking costs and benefits rather than to invoke “we have already spent so much.”

Marginal analysis is easy to state and hard to do, because marginal effects are rarely observed. Organizations know what a function costs in total and only guess what one more person would change. The guess deserves the same scrutiny as any forecast in [the next lesson](#w10-l4): a reference class, a range and an explicit statement of what would show it to be wrong.

Contribution-margin thinking also has a trap. If every incremental decision is judged only against variable cost, prices drift down and fixed costs are never covered — the airline that fills every seat at $79 goes bankrupt. Marginal pricing is right for genuinely spare capacity; it is wrong as a standing policy. The same holds for staffing: a department that accepts every “small” extra task because it uses existing people eventually discovers that its people were not spare.

challenge.title: Methodological note: allocated overhead and unit economics

blocks.text: Allocated overhead can make a profitable activity look unprofitable. Suppose a service line earns $500 thousand of revenue, has $300 thousand of variable costs and is allocated $250 thousand of shared overhead. It reports a $50 thousand loss. If the overhead will not disappear when the line closes, closing it removes $200 thousand of contribution while the $250 thousand of cost is reallocated to the remaining lines — the organization becomes $200 thousand worse off, and the other lines now look less profitable, inviting the next closure. This “death spiral” is why decisions should use avoidable costs, not allocations.

Unit economics apply the same logic to customers. A subscription business with $100 of monthly revenue per customer, an 80% gross margin and 2% monthly churn earns an undiscounted lifetime margin of 80 ÷ 0.02 = $4,000 per customer. Discounting at 1% per month, with margin received at the end of each month a customer remains, the lifetime value is 80 ÷ (0.02 + 0.01) ≈ $2,667. Against a customer acquisition cost of $1,500 the ratio is 2.7 undiscounted but only 1.8 discounted — a material difference that pitch decks often omit. The formula also assumes churn is constant, which early cohorts rarely confirm.

apply.text: Hypothetical illustration from technology: a product team wants to keep maintaining an old feature used by 4% of customers because “we spent eighteen months building it.” The relevant comparison is the engineering hours it consumes each quarter against what those hours would build elsewhere, plus any customer losses from removing it. Framed that way, the team can decide on evidence rather than loyalty to past effort.

Hypothetical illustration from the military: a service debates extending the life of an aging aircraft fleet versus buying a replacement. The original procurement cost is sunk. What matters is the future cost per flight hour of the old fleet (rising maintenance, availability), the full cost of the replacement and the capability each provides. Opportunity cost appears as the other programs the replacement budget would displace.

Opportunity cost is especially easy to neglect for staff time, because salaries are fixed and feel free. If an analyst spends ten hours a week on a manual report, the cost is not a quarter of her salary; it is the most valuable project she is not doing. One practical tool is a quarterly capacity ledger: list the department’s scarce hours, what currently consumes them, and the best unfunded use. Any new request must name which line it displaces.

Professional application in player development: a department’s scarcest resource is usually expert attention — coaches’ and analysts’ hours with players — not cash. Two applications follow. First, cost averages such as “development cost per player” say little about the value of one more instructor at a particular affiliate; ask what that person would change at the margin, for which players. Second, a hypothesis worth testing in your own organization’s records: if sunk-cost reasoning operates in talent decisions, players who received larger acquisition costs may receive more opportunities than their performance alone would predict. Treat this as a question for your data, not a conclusion, and remember that larger investments may also reflect information about talent.

APERTURE conjecture, labelled as such: departments that require every proposal to name its displaced alternative will approve fewer projects but realize more value per approved dollar. This follows from the opportunity-cost-neglect findings, but it has not, to our knowledge, been tested in organizational budgeting, and a simple before-and-after comparison in your own budget cycle would not settle it.

items: What changes if we say yes — which costs and benefits are incremental, avoidable and still ahead of us?
What has already been spent, and does any of it have salvage or reuse value that differs between options?
Which scarce resource (money, hours, attention) does this consume, and what is its best alternative use?

retain.text: Decide at the margin: count only incremental, future, avoidable costs and benefits. Contribution margin and break-even volume show how an activity’s economics change with volume. Sunk costs are irrelevant except for salvage value; allocated overhead is often unavoidable; opportunity cost is real even when no invoice records it. Under a binding budget, maximize total NPV across feasible combinations, not project by project.
In the imaging example, what volume makes the evening shift break even if reimbursement falls to $350?
Why did ranking by profitability index fail in the $1,000 budget example, and when would it have worked?
Name one recurring commitment in your area that would not survive the question “what does this displace?”

takeaways: Contribution margin (price minus variable cost) and break-even volume answer most “should we add this?” questions.
Only incremental, future, avoidable costs are relevant; sunk costs matter only through salvage or reuse value.
Opportunity cost — especially of staff time — is real but neglected unless the alternative is named.
Under capital rationing, maximize total NPV within the budget; profitability-index ranking is exact only for divisible projects.

check.prompt: A clinic is considering a new weekend service. Each visit brings $180 of revenue and $60 of variable cost. Opening on weekends adds $14,400 of fixed cost per month. How many visits per month are needed to break even?
check.working: Contribution margin per visit = 180 − 60 = $120. Break-even volume = fixed cost ÷ contribution margin = 14,400 ÷ 120 = 120 visits per month.
check.explanation: Each visit contributes $120 toward the $14,400 of fixed cost; 120 visits cover it exactly. Volume above 120 produces profit at $120 per visit; volume below produces a loss.

check.prompt: A department bought a $600,000 analytics system two years ago. It is barely used. A new system would cost $400,000 and is expected to produce benefits worth $650,000 in present value; the old system could be sold for $50,000 if replaced. Which statement correctly frames the decision?

options.text: Keep the old system: replacing it would waste $600,000.
Replace only if the new system’s benefits exceed $1,000,000, the total of old and new costs.
Compare the new system’s incremental value with the old system’s remaining value: the $600,000 is sunk, and the $50,000 resale is relevant.
The decision cannot be made until the $600,000 has been fully depreciated.

check.explanation: The $600,000 is sunk and cannot be recovered by either choice. What differs between the options is the new system’s cost and benefits, the resale value of the old system, and whatever benefit the old system would still provide if kept. Depreciation schedules do not change the economics.

optionFeedback.a: This is the sunk-cost fallacy: past spending cannot be recovered by keeping the system.
optionFeedback.b: Adding the sunk $600,000 to the hurdle double-counts a cost that both options share.
optionFeedback.d: Depreciation is an accounting allocation of a past cost; it does not change future cash flows from the choice.

check.prompt: With a $1,000 budget, projects cost and return NPV as follows: A (600, 180), B (400, 140), C (500, 160), D (300, 75). Projects cannot be split. Which set maximizes total NPV?

options.text: B and C, because they have the two highest profitability indexes.
A and B.
A and D.
B, C and D.

check.explanation: A and B cost exactly $1,000 and return $320 of NPV. B and C return $300 and leave $100 unused; A and D return $255; B, C and D cost $1,200, over budget. With indivisible projects, check combinations rather than relying on a ranking.

optionFeedback.a: Ranking by profitability index is exact only when projects are divisible; here it leaves budget stranded and yields $300, not $320.

optionFeedback.d: B, C and D cost $1,200, which exceeds the budget.

lessons.title: Valuation Under Uncertainty: Scenarios, Options and the Outside View
lessons.summary: A single forecast is a guess; scenario and sensitivity analysis expose what drives value, real options price flexibility, and reference-class forecasting corrects the optimism built into base cases.
objectives: Build sensitivity and scenario analyses and compute expected NPV and its dispersion.
Explain why a base case is usually not the expected case and why expected value is not the whole story about risk.
Value simple real options — to wait, stage or abandon — with a two-branch example.
Apply reference-class forecasting to a proposal and evaluate the dispute over why forecasts go wrong.
lessons.executive: Every investment case contains a forecast, and forecasts built from the plan itself are systematically optimistic. Three disciplines protect you. Sensitivity and scenario analysis show which assumptions actually move the answer, so debate goes where it matters. Real-options thinking values the ability to stage, wait or stop, which a static NPV ignores and which often favors pilots over big launches. Reference-class forecasting replaces the inside view of the plan with the track record of comparable projects. Ask for the distribution of outcomes, not one number; ask what the reference class says; and design projects so that you learn before you commit the bulk of the money.

explore.text: Look at the last three significant projects your organization approved. For each, ask a simple question: was the approved budget the median outcome — as likely to come in under as over — or was it the outcome if things went roughly to plan? Many people, answering honestly, realize the approved number was closer to the second. A plan describes what happens when the plan works. The distribution of what actually happens includes delays, scope changes, staff turnover, vendor problems and the occasional pleasant surprise.

Before reading on: think of a project you led or watched closely. Write down its original budget and timeline, then its actual cost and completion date. What would you have needed to know at the start to forecast the actual outcome?

Kahneman and Lovallo argued that managerial decisions combine two opposing errors. Forecasts are too bold because decision-makers adopt an **inside view**, anchored on the specifics of the plan, and neglect the statistics of similar past cases — the **outside view**. Choices are too timid because each risky option is evaluated in isolation rather than as one of many bets whose risks partly cancel. Both errors come from treating the decision at hand as unique.

understand.text: Sensitivity, scenarios and expected value

Take a synthetic proposal. Pallister Health (fictional) is considering a $2.0 million telehealth platform expected to generate $600,000 a year of net cash benefit for five years. At a 9% discount rate the five-year annuity factor is about 3.88965, so the benefits are worth about $2,333,791 and the NPV is about $333,791. That single number hides everything interesting.

understand.caption: Sensitivity analysis: change one input at a time (NPV, base case $333,791)
understand.note: Synthetic data. Rows are ordered by the size of the swing, as in a tornado chart.

understand.text: The sensitivity table ranks assumptions by how much they move the answer. Here the benefit estimate and the useful life dominate; a two-point change in the discount rate, which finance meetings often spend the most time on, matters least. Break-even analysis sharpens the point: NPV falls to zero if annual benefits are about $514,185, only 14.3% below the base case. That is the number to put in front of the decision-makers: “this project is worth doing if benefits come within 14% of plan.”

Sensitivity analysis moves one input at a time; **scenario analysis** moves several together in coherent stories, because inputs are linked — low adoption usually means lower benefits and a longer ramp. Suppose the team defines three scenarios: low (benefits 30% below plan), base, and high (20% above plan), with probabilities of 25%, 50% and 25%.

understand.caption: Pallister telehealth NPV by scenario (in $ thousands)

understand.text: Two lessons follow. First, the expected NPV of about $275,446 is lower than the base case, because the downside scenario is larger than the upside. Base cases are usually built as “the plan works,” which is not the same as the probability-weighted average. Second, expected value is not the whole story. The standard deviation of NPV across these scenarios is about $416,665, and there is a one-in-four chance, by the team’s own estimate, of destroying about $366,000. Whether that is acceptable depends on the organization’s ability to absorb losses and on how many similar bets it makes: a hospital system making dozens of such investments can rely on averages; a small clinic betting its reserves cannot.

blocks.text: Expected value is the probability-weighted average of outcomes: Σ (probability × outcome). It is the right summary when a decision is repeated many times or when outcomes are small relative to resources. Dispersion — measured by variance, standard deviation or simply the worst plausible case — describes how far outcomes may stray from that average. Two projects with the same expected NPV can differ greatly in risk: one might always return close to $200,000, another might return either −$500,000 or +$900,000 with equal chance. Because NPV is linear in cash flows, scaling all inflows by the expected multiplier gives the same expected NPV as averaging the scenarios; nonlinear features such as contract penalties or the option to stop break this shortcut.

understand.text: Real options: the value of being able to change course

Standard NPV assumes a now-or-never commitment. Real projects often allow managers to wait, stage, expand or abandon as they learn. These choices are called **real options**, by analogy with financial options: the right, but not the obligation, to take an action later. Flexibility has value whenever uncertainty will be partly resolved and the investment is costly to reverse.

understand.caption: Worked example: invest now, or pilot first? (rate 9%)
rows: Demand turns out high (benefits $800k a year for 5 years) or low ($300k a year), each with probability 50%
If demand is low, after investing
Pilot for one year ($150k), then invest only if demand is high
Invest $2.0M at year 1 if high; benefits years 2–6
understand.note: Synthetic data. Assumptions: the pilot reveals demand perfectly; delay does not change the cost or the size of the benefits; the pilot itself produces no benefit.

understand.text: Piloting is worth about $220,656 more than investing now, even though it delays benefits by a year and costs $150,000 that a confident planner would call wasted. The value comes from avoiding the low-demand branch, where investing destroys $833,105. The general pattern: options are most valuable when uncertainty is high, the decision is hard to reverse, and waiting or piloting will actually reveal information. They are worth little when delay forfeits the opportunity — for example, when a competitor will take the market — and the example’s assumptions should be challenged on exactly that point.
Reference-class forecasting: taking the outside view

steps.label: Identify the class
steps.text: Choose past projects similar enough to inform this one (same kind of system, scale, organization type).

steps.label: Establish the distribution
steps.text: Collect actual outcomes for that class — cost overruns, adoption rates, delays — as a distribution, not an average.

steps.label: Position and adjust
steps.text: Place the new project in that distribution; adjust only for specific, documented reasons it differs.

understand.text: Flyvbjerg developed reference-class forecasting as a practical application of the outside view and described its first use in planning practice: cost forecasts for large UK transport investments, including the Edinburgh Tram and London’s Crossrail. He attributes systematic forecast errors to two causes — **optimism bias**, an unintentional cognitive tendency, and **strategic misrepresentation**, deliberate understatement of costs or overstatement of benefits to win approval — and argues that basing forecasts on a reference class sidesteps both.

**Survivorship bias** compounds the problem. Benchmarks, vendor case studies and “best practice” stories come disproportionately from projects and firms that succeeded and are still around to be studied. A reference class built only from survivors overstates success rates. When a vendor says “clients like you saw a 30% improvement,” ask how many clients like you bought the product and what happened to the ones you are not hearing about.

challenge.text: The explanation for forecast errors is disputed. Love and Ahiaga-Dagbui argue that framing cost underestimation in transport projects as either honest error or deliberate lie is a false dichotomy when set against how large infrastructure is actually procured, describe the conclusions of influential earlier work by Flyvbjerg and colleagues as unfounded, and urge evidence-based approaches to setting cost estimates. Flyvbjerg has replied that this view will keep planners getting costs wrong. The dispute concerns why estimates go wrong, and therefore what fixes them. For an executive, two practical points follow: reference-class forecasting can be useful whichever explanation is right, because it corrects the forecast without needing to diagnose motives; and any claimed overrun depends on its baseline — an “overrun” measured from an early concept estimate looks much larger than one measured from a final contract price — so the baseline must be explicit before a claim about bias is accepted.

Reference-class forecasting has its own limits. Choosing the class is a judgment, and a motivated analyst can pick a flattering one. Small organizations may have only a handful of comparable past projects, and genuinely novel initiatives may have no meaningful class at all. The method also assumes the past distribution is a fair guide to the future; if the organization has genuinely improved its project management, the reference class will be too pessimistic. The remedy is transparency: state the class, its size and why it fits, and show what the forecast would be under a reasonable alternative class.

Real-options language is easily abused. Almost any project can be said to “create options,” and “strategic value” can be invoked to rescue proposals whose cash flows do not justify them. An option is valuable only if three conditions hold: uncertainty will actually be resolved, the organization will genuinely act on what it learns (including stopping), and keeping the option open costs less than it is worth. Organizations that never cancel pilots do not own abandonment options; they own slow launches.

challenge.title: Methodological note: Monte Carlo simulation, correlation and risk adjustment

blocks.text: Monte Carlo simulation replaces three scenarios with thousands of random draws from distributions for each input, producing a full distribution of NPV. Its value depends entirely on the input distributions and, critically, on their correlations: if adoption and benefit per user are both driven by the same underlying demand, simulating them independently understates risk. A simulation that looks precise but assumes independence is more misleading than three honest scenarios.

There are two standard ways to recognize risk in valuation: adjust the discount rate upward for riskier cash flows, or adjust the cash flows themselves toward certainty-equivalent values and discount at a lower rate. Either can be defended; using both for the same risk double-counts it. Introductory finance texts cover the first route through the cost of capital; the second requires an explicit judgment about how much certainty the organization would trade for expected value.

apply.text: Hypothetical illustration from government technology: a state agency replacing a benefits-eligibility system receives a vendor estimate of 18 months and $40 million. A reference-class review of the agency’s and peer agencies’ past system replacements shows that most took substantially longer and cost more than first estimated. The agency budgets a contingency drawn from that distribution and, more importantly, restructures the contract into stages with go/no-go reviews — buying abandonment options it previously lacked.

Hypothetical illustration from venture investing and drug development: both fields are built on staged commitments. A venture fund invests a small amount, learns, and invests more only in companies that hit milestones; a pharmaceutical firm funds a compound through successive trial phases, each a decision point. In both, the expected value of any single early bet is often negative on a static view, and the portfolio is designed around the option to stop.

apply.title: Executive twist: “The board wants one number”

blocks.text: Your board chair asks for “the number” for a major facility investment. Giving a single figure invites false precision; refusing invites the perception that you do not know. A practical compromise is three sentences: the expected NPV; the range within which you are, say, 80% confident; and the one assumption that would flip the decision, with your plan for learning it early. Boards rarely object to uncertainty that is quantified and paired with a plan to reduce it; they object to surprises.

apply.text: Professional application in baseball operations: suppose an organization considers building a new player development technology center. A reference class is available — the organization’s own past facility and technology projects and, informally, peers’ — and should be assembled before the vendor’s estimate is accepted. The real-option design question is whether the center can be staged: equip one affiliate first, measure usage and player outcomes for a season, then expand. Staging costs a year of benefits at the other affiliates; it buys protection against the low-adoption branch, which the organization’s own reference class may well show is not rare. The same structure applies to international development initiatives and to research partnerships.

items: Which two or three assumptions drive most of the NPV, and what is the break-even value of each?
Is the base case the median outcome or the “plan works” outcome?
What does a reference class of comparable past projects say about cost, timing and adoption — and who chose the class?
Can the project be staged, piloted or abandoned, and will we actually stop if early results disappoint?
Can we absorb the downside scenario, or is this a bet we cannot afford to lose?

retain.text: Sensitivity analysis finds the assumptions that matter; scenario analysis combines them into coherent stories and yields an expected NPV that is usually below the base case. Expected value does not capture risk; dispersion and the size of the downside relative to resources do. Real options value the ability to learn before committing, but only if the organization will act on what it learns. Reference-class forecasting corrects inside-view optimism, though the causes of forecast error remain disputed.
Why is the Pallister expected NPV ($275,446) lower than its base-case NPV ($333,791)?
State the three conditions under which a real option has meaningful value.
Name a reference class you could assemble for a decision you face this year. How many cases would it contain, and who would object to it?

Base cases are usually “plan works” outcomes, so expected NPV is often lower; expected value also ignores the size of the downside.
Real options — to stage, wait or abandon — can be worth more than they cost when uncertainty will resolve and you will act on it.
Reference-class forecasting replaces the inside view with the track record of comparable projects; why forecasts fail is still debated.

check.prompt: A project has three scenarios: NPV of −$400,000 with probability 0.3, $200,000 with probability 0.5 and $900,000 with probability 0.2. What is its expected NPV, in dollars?
check.explanation: Expected value weights each scenario’s NPV by its probability and sums: −$120,000 + $100,000 + $180,000 = $160,000. It sits below the most likely outcome of $200,000 because the probability-weighted shortfall of the low case (0.3 × 600,000 = 180,000) exceeds the weighted gain of the high case (0.2 × 700,000 = 140,000). The 30% chance of losing $400,000 must still be judged against what the organization can absorb.

check.prompt: Under which conditions is the option to pilot a project before full rollout most valuable?

options.text: Low uncertainty, an easily reversible investment, and a pilot that reveals little.
High uncertainty, a costly-to-reverse investment, a pilot that reveals what you need to know, and willingness to stop.
Whenever the static NPV is negative, because options can always rescue a project.
When a competitor is likely to capture the opportunity during the pilot.

check.explanation: Flexibility is worth most when outcomes are uncertain, commitment is hard to undo, waiting resolves the uncertainty, and the organization will actually act on the result — including stopping. Without those conditions, a pilot mainly delays benefits.

optionFeedback.a: With little uncertainty, little to learn and easy reversal, there is almost nothing for a pilot to protect against.
optionFeedback.c: Options add value only under specific conditions; invoking them to rescue any negative-NPV project is a common abuse.
optionFeedback.d: If delay forfeits the opportunity, the cost of waiting rises and the option to pilot is worth less.

check.prompt: A vendor’s proposal for a new scheduling system assumes 90% of staff will use it within a year. Which step best applies reference-class forecasting?

options.text: Ask the vendor for a more detailed implementation plan to test the 90% figure.

Average the vendor’s 90% with your team’s own estimate of 70%.
Raise the discount rate to reflect the uncertainty about adoption.

check.explanation: Reference-class forecasting takes the outside view: it bases the forecast on the actual outcomes of a class of comparable past projects and adjusts only for documented differences. A more detailed plan, however careful, is still the inside view.

optionFeedback.a: More detail about this plan deepens the inside view; it does not reveal how similar plans actually turned out.
optionFeedback.c: Averaging two inside-view estimates does not introduce base-rate information.
optionFeedback.d: Adjusting the rate is a blunt risk adjustment; it does not correct a biased adoption assumption.
