lessons.title: Paying for Wins: The Economics of Talent Spending
lessons.summary: Talent spending is capital allocation under uncertainty: value it as surplus over cost, at the margin, against an explicit objective — and expect any pricing edge to erode.
objectives: Explain marginal revenue product and why the value of an additional win is nonlinear.
Compute and interpret cost per marginal win and surplus value, and state their limits.
Evaluate evidence on mispricing in sports labor markets, including the dispute over the NFL draft “loser’s curse.”
Build and stress-test a business case for development spending expressed in surplus value.
lessons.executive: A sports organization’s largest investments are people, and the same logic that values a machine values a player or a coach: expected future contribution, priced at the margin, net of cost, discounted for time and risk. Two complications dominate. The value of a win is not constant — it concentrates near thresholds such as playoff qualification — so efficiency ratios can mislead. And talent markets can misprice skills, but research shows such edges erode once rivals learn, and whether a price is “too high” depends on the objective you hold. Ask every talent proposal for its surplus over cost, the objective it serves and how long any edge will last.

explore.text: Picture a league table sorted by payroll efficiency — wins per dollar spent. The club at the top need not be the one with the largest payroll, and it may not be a contender at all. A common reaction is that the big spenders are wasting money. An economist would ask a different question: what is the next win worth to each club? For a club on the edge of the postseason, a few additional wins can be worth far more than the same wins to a club certain to finish in last place or certain to qualify.

Before reading on: estimate, in rough terms, whether an additional win is worth more to a club projected for 72 wins or one projected for 87 wins in a league where about 88 wins usually qualify for the postseason. What would make your answer wrong?

Talent spending is capital allocation. Signing a player, hiring a coach or funding a development program commits money now in exchange for an uncertain stream of future contribution. Every tool from this week applies: discounting, marginal analysis, opportunity cost, scenarios and reference classes. What is distinctive about sports is that output is measured in wins, wins are relative to rivals, and the money value of a win depends on where the club stands.

understand.text: Marginal revenue product and the value of a win

In labor economics, a worker’s **marginal revenue product** is the additional revenue the organization earns from employing that worker: the worker’s marginal product (here, additional wins) multiplied by the marginal revenue of that output (the revenue an additional win brings). A rational employer would pay up to the marginal revenue product; the difference between that value and the pay is the employer’s surplus.

understand.caption: Illustrative marginal revenue of one additional win, by a club’s win total ($ millions)
understand.note: Synthetic. A teaching illustration of a nonlinear win-value curve in a league where about 88 wins usually qualify for the postseason; not an estimate for any real league.

understand.text: The shape matters more than the numbers. If additional wins are worth most near the qualification threshold, then the same player is worth more to a contender than to a rebuilding club, and the same club should value talent differently from one season to the next. This is why rebuilding clubs trade veterans to contenders: the trade can create value for both sides because the player’s marginal revenue product differs between them.
Cost per marginal win

understand.caption: Payroll efficiency in a fictional 162-game league (replacement-level baseline: $60M payroll ≈ 45 wins)
understand.note: Synthetic data. Cost per marginal win = (payroll − 60) ÷ (wins − 45).

understand.text: Cost per marginal win divides spending above a replacement-level baseline by wins above that baseline. Club E is strikingly efficient at about $0.42 million per marginal win; Club A spends about $2.98 million. But an average ratio says little about the marginal decision. Club A’s last few wins carried it from the high 80s into the low 90s, the band where, on the illustrative curve, each win is worth $2.5–3.5 million. Its spending may have been rational even though its average efficiency is poor. Club E, at 81 wins, might have gained more from spending to reach the threshold than from protecting its ratio. Efficiency is a property of the whole roster; value is created at the margin.
Mispricing and surplus value: what the evidence shows

Hakes and Sauer tested the claim, popularized by the book Moneyball, that baseball’s labor market mispriced skills. Using player productivity and salary data from 1999 to 2004, they estimated how batting skills contributed to winning and how each was paid. On-base percentage contributed more to winning than salaries reflected before the book appeared; once the idea spread, the pricing gap largely disappeared. The finding illustrates both halves of the lesson: talent markets can be inefficient, and inefficiencies that can be observed tend to be competed away.

Massey and Thaler examined the National Football League draft, comparing the price of draft picks — what teams give up for them in draft-day trades — with the **surplus value** drafted players deliver, defined as performance value minus compensation. They found that top picks are significantly overvalued: the very earliest picks yield less surplus on average than later first-round picks, a pattern they argue is inconsistent with efficient markets and consistent with behavioral explanations such as overconfidence.

Surplus value explains why player development matters economically. In leagues where early-career pay is constrained by collectively bargained rules, a player developed internally can deliver major-league-quality performance for several seasons at well below market pay. The surplus over those seasons is the return on the development investment, and it can exceed what the same money would buy on the open market. The difficulty is not the logic but the measurement: the uplift any program produces is small relative to the noise in player outcomes.

understand.caption: Worked example: valuing one year of additional development spending
rows: Assumed uplift: additional players reaching a 2-win-per-season level
understand.note: Synthetic data and assumptions for illustration; the win price, uplift, salary and timing are not estimates for any real league or club.

understand.text: The worked example produces a striking result: the program breaks even if each year of spending produces just 0.088 additional useful players — fewer than one per decade of spending. That sounds like an easy case. But read it through this week’s lens. The answer is driven almost entirely by two assumptions — the uplift and the price of a win — neither of which can be observed directly, and an uplift of 0.1 player a year would be practically impossible to detect in a single organization’s outcomes, which are dominated by noise. The business case therefore rests on evidence about mechanisms and intermediate outcomes, not on the headline NPV.

understand.title: Prerequisite: marginal product and marginal revenue

blocks.text: Marginal product is the extra output from one more unit of an input, holding others fixed: the additional wins from one more good player, or the additional cases closed by one more paralegal. It usually diminishes as more of the input is added, because other inputs become the constraint. Marginal revenue is the extra revenue from one more unit of output. Multiply the two and you get the most an employer should be willing to pay for that input. Every hiring decision in any industry is an estimate of this product, made with incomplete information.

challenge.text: Whether a price is “too high” depends on the objective. Brill and Wyner re-examined the loser’s curse and argued that Massey and Thaler’s conclusion hinges on assuming teams should maximize expected surplus value. If outcomes are highly skewed and a transformational player is disproportionately valuable — for example, because championships depend on a few elite players — then a team that prioritizes the chance of landing such a player may rationally pay a premium for top picks. Massey and Thaler’s evidence about prices and average surplus stands; what is disputed is whether average surplus is the right yardstick. The general lesson for executives is to state the objective — expected wins, championship probability, profit, development throughput — before calling any talent decision efficient or wasteful.

Edges erode. The Hakes and Sauer findings show a mispricing that disappeared once the underlying insight became public. Any advantage built on a measurable, imitable insight should be valued over a short horizon, and its value is highest before rivals notice. Sustained advantage is more likely to come from capabilities that are hard to copy — integrated development systems, culture, relationships — which are also the hardest to value in a spreadsheet.

Three further cautions. First, wins are relative: one club’s additional win is another’s loss, so league-wide spending races can raise costs without raising anyone’s expected wins. Second, competitive bidding for talent invites the winner’s curse: when many bidders estimate a player’s value with error, the highest bidder is disproportionately likely to be the one who overestimated. Third, payroll and wins correlate partly because winning raises revenue that funds payroll, so cross-club comparisons cannot establish how many wins an extra dollar buys.

challenge.title: Methodological note: estimating the value of a win

blocks.text: Estimating marginal revenue per win typically means regressing club revenue on wins, playoff appearances and controls such as market size, often with lagged wins, because attendance and sponsorship respond to past success. Three problems recur. Reverse causality: revenue funds payroll, which produces wins. Omitted variables: market size, stadium quality and ownership objectives drive both revenue and spending. Nonlinearity: a linear model averages steep threshold effects into a misleading constant. Credible estimates therefore use within-club variation over time, model thresholds explicitly and report wide intervals. When someone quotes a single “price of a win,” ask which method produced it, over which years, and whether it is an average or a marginal figure.

apply.text: Hypothetical illustration from European football: in leagues with promotion and relegation, the marginal revenue of points near the relegation line can be enormous, because dropping a division sharply cuts broadcast income. A club near the line may rationally spend heavily for a few points that would be worth little to a mid-table club. The same nonlinear logic as the playoff threshold, with a cliff instead of a step.

Hypothetical illustration from technology and law: a software company weighing one senior engineer against two junior engineers, or a law firm weighing a lateral partner hire, faces the same questions. What is the marginal product of this person in this team, how much of their past output was produced by their former organization’s systems, and is the price inflated because several bidders competed? A firm that wins a bidding contest for a star on the strength of past numbers should expect some disappointment for exactly that reason: the winning bid is the one most likely to have overestimated.

apply.title: Executive twist: “Why not spend $20 million more?”

blocks.text: An owner asks why the club does not add $20 million of payroll to chase a title. A useful answer has four parts, none of which requires precise data. Where are we on the win-value curve — is the next win worth a lot or a little? What is the realistic marginal product of $20 million in the current market, given that late-season talent is expensive and contested? What is the opportunity cost — the development, facilities or future flexibility that money would otherwise fund? And what objective are we optimizing this year: championship probability, long-run competitiveness or financial results? Laying out those four questions turns a contest of opinions into a decision.

apply.text: Professional application in player development: a department competing for budget should express its proposals in the club’s language of value — surplus over cost — while being candid about uncertainty. A credible case states the mechanism (what will change in which players’ development), the intermediate measures that should move within a season (skill metrics, durability, availability), the assumption chain that converts those into expected surplus, and the break-even uplift. Because outcome data will be too noisy to confirm the uplift for years, agree in advance on the leading indicators that would justify continuing, expanding or stopping. That pre-commitment protects the department from both premature cancellation and sunk-cost persistence.

items: What objective is this talent investment serving, and who agreed to it?
What is the expected surplus over cost, and which two assumptions drive it?
Where is the organization on its value curve, and does that make the margin unusually valuable or unusually cheap?
How long will any pricing edge last once rivals notice?
Which leading indicators, agreed in advance, will decide whether to continue?

retain.text: Value talent as surplus over cost: marginal product times the marginal value of output, minus pay, discounted for time and risk. The value of a win is nonlinear, so average efficiency ratios mislead about marginal decisions. Research shows talent markets can misprice skills and that such edges erode; whether a price is too high depends on the objective, which must be stated. Development spending earns its return through surplus in cost-controlled years, but the uplift is hard to measure, so pre-agreed leading indicators matter.
Why can a trade of a veteran from a rebuilding club to a contender create value for both clubs?
In the development worked example, which two assumptions drive the NPV, and what is the break-even uplift?
State the objective your own organization appears to optimize when it spends on talent. Is it written down anywhere?

takeaways: Marginal revenue product — marginal wins times the marginal value of a win — is the ceiling on what talent is worth to an organization.
Win value is nonlinear around thresholds, so average cost-per-win ratios mislead about marginal decisions.
Talent markets can misprice skills, but observable edges erode once rivals learn.
Whether a price is “too high” depends on the stated objective; specify it before judging efficiency.
Development spending creates surplus in cost-controlled seasons; pre-agree leading indicators because outcomes are noisy.

check.prompt: In a fictional league, a replacement-level roster costs $60 million and wins 45 games. A club with a $130 million payroll wins 85 games. What is its cost per marginal win, in $ millions? Round to two decimals.
check.working: Payroll above baseline = 130 − 60 = $70 million. Wins above baseline = 85 − 45 = 40. Cost per marginal win = 70 ÷ 40 = $1.75 million.
check.explanation: Cost per marginal win divides spending above a replacement-level baseline by wins above that baseline: 70 ÷ 40 = 1.75. It is an average over all the club’s marginal wins, so it does not tell you what the next win would cost or be worth.

optionFeedback.c: The study documents an inefficiency, so markets were not always efficient.
optionFeedback.d: The study reports that the gap largely disappeared after the insight spread.

glossary.definition: Recording revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred to produce that revenue, regardless of when cash changes hands.
The statement of performance over a period: revenues minus expenses, on an accrual basis, equal net income.
The statement of position at a moment: assets equal liabilities plus owners’ equity.
The statement that explains the change in cash over a period, split into operating, investing and financing activities, and reconciles accrual profit to cash.
Current assets minus current liabilities; increases in receivables and inventory absorb cash, increases in payables release it.
Commonly, cash from operations minus capital expenditure: the cash available to lenders and owners after maintaining and growing the asset base.
The sum of all of a project’s cash flows, each discounted to today at the opportunity cost of capital, including the initial outlay; positive NPV means the project beats its alternative.
The discount rate at which a project’s NPV equals zero; useful as a summary but unreliable for ranking mutually exclusive projects or non-conventional cash flows.
The time until cumulative cash inflows recover the initial outlay; discounted payback uses discounted cash flows. It ignores cash after the cutoff.
The blended required return of a firm’s lenders (after tax) and owners, weighted by their shares of financing; the right discount rate only for projects of average risk.
The present value of a project’s future cash flows divided by its initial cost; ranking by it is exact under capital rationing only when projects are divisible.
Price minus variable cost per unit: what each additional unit contributes to fixed costs and profit. Fixed costs divided by it give break-even volume.
A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered under any option; irrelevant to the decision except through any salvage or reuse value.
The value of the best alternative forgone by a choice, including alternative uses of scarce staff time; real even though no invoice records it.
Allocating a fixed budget among positive-NPV projects that cannot all be funded, by maximizing total NPV across feasible combinations.

Sensitivity analysis changes one assumption at a time to see which drive value; scenario analysis changes several together in coherent stories, often weighted by probability to give an expected value.
The right, but not the obligation, to take a future action on a real investment — to wait, stage, expand or abandon — whose value rises with uncertainty and irreversibility.
Forecasting a project’s cost, timing or results from the actual outcomes of a class of comparable past projects (the outside view), then adjusting only for documented differences.
The additional revenue from employing one more unit of an input: its marginal product (such as wins) times the marginal revenue of that output.
The value of a person’s performance to the organization minus what the organization pays them; the return on talent and development investments.

exercise.title: Capital Allocation Lab

intro.text: You chair the capital committee of Marrowfield Regional Health, a fictional regional hospital system. Seven projects compete for a $5.0 million capital budget; together they would cost $8.2 million. Your job is to choose a portfolio, defend it, and discover how much the answer depends on the discount rate, the scenarios and the things the cash flows leave out.

items: Start at the default 8% rate. Before selecting anything, predict which three projects the lab will rank highest by NPV, by IRR and by payback.
Select a portfolio within the budget. Compare it with the lab’s best portfolio by enumeration and note the opportunity cost of any difference.
Move the rate to 5%, 12% and 16%. Watch which projects change sign and when the best portfolio changes.
Switch to the low and high scenarios. Note which projects are fragile and which are robust.
Decide what to do about the community clinic, whose value is mostly outside the cash flows. Write down the NPV you are willing to give up for it, and why.

intro.text: Everything here is synthetic. The lab computes every number from the cash flows shown, using the formulas it displays; it does not predict what would happen in any real hospital.

brief.text: Marrowfield Regional Health (fictional) operates two hospitals and a network of outpatient sites. The board has approved a $5.0 million capital budget for the coming year and will not increase it. Finance estimates the system’s cost of capital at 8% and applies it to every project unless the committee decides otherwise. Projects cannot be split or phased within this exercise: each is all or nothing.

Cash flows are net incremental cash flows in dollars for year 0 (the investment) and each following year: new revenue or savings minus new operating costs, before financing. The low, base and high scenarios multiply all inflows by the factors shown; the investment itself does not change.

projects.label: Patient scheduling and reminder software
projects.description: Replace the phone-based scheduling process with online booking and automated reminders across outpatient sites.
projects.notes: Savings come from fewer missed appointments and less scheduling staff time. Benefits decline from year 3 because the vendor plans a new platform that would require another purchase.
projects.nonfinancial: Better patient access and experience; scheduling staff could be redeployed to patient navigation rather than laid off, if leadership chooses.

projects.label: Outpatient surgery wing expansion
projects.description: Add four procedure rooms to the main campus’s outpatient surgery center.
projects.notes: Volume ramps over four years as surgeons are recruited. The low scenario reflects slower recruitment and payer pressure on reimbursement; the high scenario reflects capturing procedures now going to a competitor.
projects.nonfinancial: Construction disruption for two years; dependence on recruiting surgeons; strategically important if outpatient procedures keep shifting away from inpatient settings.

projects.label: Revenue-cycle automation
projects.description: Automate claims scrubbing and denial follow-up in the billing office.
projects.notes: Benefits come from faster collection and fewer written-off denials. The vendor contract ends after three years; renewal terms are unknown.
projects.nonfinancial: Reduces billing backlog that frustrates patients; may reduce billing staff over time, which the committee must handle with care.

projects.label: Community clinic in an underserved neighborhood
projects.description: Open a primary-care clinic in a neighborhood with no nearby primary care.
projects.notes: Patient revenue covers most operating costs but not the investment. Possible public grants and downstream referrals to the system’s hospitals are not included because neither is committed.
projects.nonfinancial: Access to care in an underserved area, alignment with the system’s community mission, and relationships with local government. These benefits are real but not in the cash flows.

projects.label: Remote patient-monitoring venture
projects.description: Launch a program that monitors patients with chronic heart failure at home after discharge.
projects.notes: Highly uncertain: depends on patient adoption, clinician workflow and reimbursement rules that may change. The wide scenario range is the team’s honest assessment, not padding.
projects.nonfinancial: Builds capability in a care model the board considers strategically important; failure would be visible to clinicians who championed it.

projects.label: Energy-efficiency retrofit
projects.description: Replace lighting, controls and chillers at the main hospital.
projects.notes: Savings are predictable and depend mainly on energy prices; engineering estimates are based on metered use.
projects.nonfinancial: Lower emissions and better resilience during heat waves; low execution risk.

projects.label: Imaging equipment replacement
projects.description: Replace an aging CT scanner with a faster model.
projects.notes: Inflows combine added scan capacity and avoided downtime and repair costs of the old machine. The old scanner’s original cost is sunk and is not included; its small resale value is netted into year 0.
projects.nonfinancial: Clinical quality and reliability; the current scanner’s failure would disrupt emergency care.

questions: At 8%, which portfolio maximizes NPV within the budget? How would ranking by IRR or by payback have changed your choice?
Move the rate to 5%, 12% and 16%. Which projects change sign, and at what rate does the best portfolio change? What does that tell you about where to focus debate?
What is the NPV cost of including the community clinic, measured against the best portfolio without it? Who should decide whether the community benefit is worth that price?
Would you include the remote-monitoring venture? How could it be restructured as a staged option, and what milestones would you require?
Which projects’ low scenarios are likely to happen together, and what does that imply about the risk of your portfolio?

key.insights: At 8% the best portfolio is scheduling software, the surgery wing, revenue-cycle automation and the imaging replacement: it uses exactly $5.0 million and yields about $1.19 million of NPV. The next best swaps imaging for remote monitoring (about $1.15 million, $4.7 million spent) but adds a high-variance bet whose low scenario loses about $764,000. The rules disagree: by IRR, revenue-cycle automation (about 21.7%) and scheduling (about 21.3%) lead and the surgery wing (about 14.0%) ranks fourth; by NPV the wing leads (about $634,000); by profitability index the wing is narrowly first (about 1.26). Payback favors the two small software projects (under two years) and would push out the wing (about 4.6 years) even though it creates the most value. The best portfolio is unchanged between 5% and 12%, so the rate matters less than it seems within that range — but at 14% the wing is roughly break-even, and at 16% only the two software projects remain positive and most of the budget goes unspent. The energy retrofit is positive only below about 6.1%: a safe project rejected by a single 8% rate, the distortion discussed in Lesson 2. Including the community clinic costs about $551,000 of NPV relative to the best portfolio (best feasible set with the clinic: wing, revenue-cycle, clinic and remote monitoring, about $639,000) — more than the clinic’s own NPV of about −$373,000, because of what it displaces. That price is a governance question for the board, not an analyst’s call. Finally, if all four chosen projects hit their low scenarios together — plausible, because the wing, imaging and scheduling all depend on patient volume — the best portfolio’s NPV falls to about −$472,000, so diversification across these projects is weaker than it looks.

debrief.text: The lab shows four things. Decision rules disagree, and NPV at the right rate is the one that measures value; IRR and payback favor small, early-paying projects. A binding budget turns every project’s cost into the NPV it displaces, which is why the clinic’s true price exceeds its own negative NPV. The discount rate matters most at the extremes and for long-lived projects; within a plausible range, scenario assumptions often matter more. And correlated risks — several projects depending on the same patient volume — make a portfolio riskier than a project-by-project view suggests.

What the lab does not show is just as important. The cash flows are synthetic forecasts and inherit every bias discussed in Lesson 4; a reference class of the system’s past projects would likely change several of them. Projects here are all-or-nothing, so the lab cannot value staging or pilots, which in practice could transform the remote-monitoring decision. Scenarios move inflows only, not costs or timing. And the community clinic’s value cannot be reduced to a number the lab can add — the lab can tell you its price, not whether it is worth paying.

Professional application: a baseball operations or player development budget has the same structure. Proposals differ in size, timing and risk; some carry mission or relationship value outside the cash flows; several depend on the same underlying driver, such as staff capacity to use new tools. Use the lab’s questions on your own next budget cycle: what does each proposal displace, which rule is ranking it, and which risks move together?

Scenario multipliers apply to inflows only; investment amounts and timing are fixed.
Projects are indivisible and independent except for the shared budget; no project can be phased within the exercise.
The budget is a hard constraint for one year; unspent funds earn nothing in this model.
Non-financial considerations are described in words and are not scored by the engine.

case.title: The Budget Decision
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. The Graniteport Harriers are an invented club; any resemblance to a real organization is unintended.

body.text: The email from Owen Halvorsen, general manager of the Graniteport Harriers, was three lines long. Ownership had approved $1.2 million of incremental spending for player development in the next fiscal year. He wanted a recommendation from Marisol Quintero, the director of player development, in three weeks, and a one-page memo he could take to the club president. “Tell me what you’d do, what you’d need to believe, and what would change your mind.”

Quintero had wanted this money for two years. The Harriers were a mid-market club that could not outspend rivals for established players, and the front office had decided that its edge would come from developing its own. Now that the money had arrived, it felt smaller than the list of things it was supposed to fix. Three proposals had reached her desk, each with an advocate she respected.

Ray Tolliver, the club’s senior pitching coordinator and a twenty-year veteran of the system, wanted four hires: two development coaches for the lowest affiliates, a sports-science coordinator to manage workloads and recovery, and a bilingual education coordinator to support players arriving from the club’s international academy. “Every tool we have is only as good as the person standing next to the player,” he said. “Our lower affiliates have the thinnest staffing in the system, and the kids who struggle most are the ones adjusting to a new country and a new language at the same time.” The four positions would cost about $780,000 a year, plus $60,000 to recruit and relocate them.

The finance office had a problem with Option A that had nothing to do with its merits. Under a policy adopted the previous year, any new recurring commitment above $700,000 a year required ownership approval at a quarterly meeting — the next one in two months. The club’s hiring window for affiliate staff, Tolliver pointed out, would close in ten weeks. A three-person version would fit under the threshold, but he did not want to choose which of the four roles to drop.

A technology vendor had pitched an integrated biomechanics capture and data platform: high-speed motion capture at every affiliate, automated reports and a player-facing app. The price was $900,000 up front, $150,000 a year in license and maintenance, and an estimated $100,000 of internal integration work in the first year. The vendor’s deck included a payback analysis of under two years and quotes from three satisfied clients. Daniel Okafor, the club’s vice president of finance, liked the option’s shape: low recurring cost, a clear asset and the best numbers of the three.

There was an awkward history. Two years earlier, Quintero herself had championed a $600,000 motion-capture lab at the spring complex. It worked as designed, but staff used it for about a third of the sessions planned. The vendor offered a $50,000 trade-in credit if the club replaced it. Quintero noticed that the idea of retiring her own lab made her want to find reasons the new platform was unnecessary, and she noticed that she did not like noticing it.

Priya Natarajan, the department’s lead analyst, proposed two research analysts and a data engineer, about $520,000 a year, plus $120,000 for computing and data infrastructure. Her pitch was not about any single tool. “We collect more data than we use,” she said. “The lab is underused because nobody has time to turn its output into something a coach can act on. If we build the capacity to run structured comparisons — this drill against that one, this workload rule against the old one — every future tool decision gets better, including this one.” She objected to the finance office’s five-year horizon: in her estimates, the benefits of research capacity were still rising in year five and would continue long after.

Okafor’s team had converted each option’s expected development benefits into dollars using the club’s internal convention — an estimate of the surplus value of additional major-league-quality player-seasons produced by the system — and discounted everything at the club’s standard 8% rate over five years (Exhibits 1–3). Halvorsen called the convention “directionally right and precisely wrong.” Everyone agreed it was the best common currency they had.

On those numbers, the technology platform looked strongest: the highest expected NPV, the fastest payback and the smallest recurring commitment. Okafor’s summary was blunt. “If we believe our own estimates, B is the answer. If we don’t believe our own estimates, we shouldn’t be using them for A and C either.”

Natarajan’s reply was a spreadsheet of her own (Exhibit 4): the club’s last six technology purchases, their budgets, their actual costs and the share of intended users actively using each one twelve months later. The median cost overrun was about 11%. The median twelve-month usage was 45%. The vendor’s case assumed 90% of intended staff would use the platform; the finance office’s base case assumed 65%; its low case assumed 45% — which, Natarajan pointed out, was not a pessimistic scenario but the club’s own typical result.

Tolliver made a different point. The lab was underused, he said, because there were not enough coaches at the lower levels to run sessions and still coach. Buying more technology without more people would repeat the problem; hiring people without better tools would waste their time. Natarajan agreed about the complementarity and disagreed about which complement mattered: analysts, not coaches, were the bottleneck. Okafor noted that the budget allowed none of the pairs anyone wanted. The platform plus either of the other options exceeded $1.2 million in the first year.

Several facts that mattered were not in any exhibit. The vendor’s sales lead had hinted, informally, that a phased deal was possible — installation at two affiliates for one season, with the rest contingent on agreed usage milestones — but at a higher total price, perhaps $80,000 more, and nothing was in writing. Nobody knew whether the platform’s adoption would be higher than the club’s past technology purchases; the vendor said its onboarding was better, which every vendor says. Nobody could say how much of the lab’s underuse was about staffing, how much about the lab’s design and how much about coaches’ skepticism. And no one could measure development benefits directly within the five-year window: the outcomes that the convention valued would take years to observe and would be dominated by noise.

There was also a question Halvorsen had not asked but would. The president had once told Quintero that she judged department heads less by whether their bets paid off than by whether they had said in advance what success would look like. A recommendation that could not specify its own failure conditions would not survive the meeting.

Quintero blocked out a Sunday to write. She had the exhibits, the three advocates’ arguments, a hard first-year budget of $1.2 million, a recurring-commitment threshold she could exceed only by waiting for ownership, a hiring window that might not wait, a lab she had bought and a suspicion that the most defensible-looking option was the one most likely to repeat the club’s past. She also knew that “do a little of everything” was the answer most likely to be approved and least likely to work.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — Cost profiles ($ thousands)
exhibits.note: Synthetic data. Assumptions: costs in nominal dollars; the first-year budget counts year-0 one-time costs plus year-1 costs; the $50,000 trade-in credit for the existing lab is not included.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — Estimated annual development benefits by scenario ($ thousands of estimated surplus value)
rows: Vendor deck; assumes 90% of intended users active
Slow hiring; little adoption of findings
exhibits.note: Synthetic data. Assumption: benefits use the club’s internal convention of $4.0 million of surplus value per additional major-league-quality player-season produced; for example, $1.15 million a year corresponds to about 0.29 such player-seasons. Benefits after year 5 are excluded by the finance office’s five-year horizon.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Finance office summary at 8% over five years ($ thousands)
exhibits.note: Synthetic data computed from Exhibits 1 and 2: net cash flow each year = benefits − costs, discounted at 8%. Scenario probabilities are the finance office’s judgment.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 4 — Reference class: the club’s last six technology purchases
exhibits.note: Synthetic data compiled by the department’s lead analyst. Usage is the share of staff the purchase was intended for who used it at least weekly.

assumptions: All figures are synthetic and in nominal dollars; the club’s standard discount rate is 8% for every project.
The finance office evaluates all options over five years with no value after year 5.
Development benefits are expressed in dollars through the club’s internal surplus-value convention, which no one can validate precisely.
The first-year budget of $1.2 million is firm; new recurring commitments above $700,000 a year require ownership approval at a meeting two months away.
The existing motion-capture lab cost $600,000 two years ago; its trade-in value is $50,000 if replaced.
A phased vendor deal may be possible at roughly $80,000 more in total, but its terms are unconfirmed.
questions: Use Exhibit 4 to adjust Option B’s forecast. Which scenario in Exhibit 2 does the club’s own reference class support, and what happens to B’s attractiveness if you also apply the median cost overrun to the upfront price?
How should the $600,000 motion-capture lab and its $50,000 trade-in value enter the analysis — and how should Quintero handle her own stake in it?
Which option, or which combination within the constraints, would you recommend? For each alternative you reject, state what someone would need to believe for it to be the better choice.
How could you restructure one option to create a real option — a pilot, a phased contract or a staged hiring plan — and what milestones would trigger expansion or exit?
The finance office uses a five-year horizon and one 8% rate for all three options. Are those choices neutral among A, B and C?

perspectives.title: Buy the platform — as an option, not a commitment
perspectives.text: B has the best expected NPV and the smallest recurring cost, and finance trusts it. The reference class is a warning, not a veto: negotiate the phased deal, install at two affiliates, and make the rest contingent on usage above the club’s 45% median. Even at about $80,000 more, the phased deal limits the downside the reference class predicts. Retire the old lab only if the pilot outperforms it. The risk: without more staff, the pilot may simply reproduce the lab’s 35% usage and the club will have learned that at a cost.

perspectives.title: People first, inside the threshold
perspectives.text: Hire three of Tolliver’s four roles now to stay under the $700,000 recurring threshold and inside the hiring window, and invest the remaining first-year money in making the existing lab usable. If benefits scale with headcount, a three-person version has a base-case NPV of roughly $156,000 on the exhibit’s assumptions; its real case is that people are the binding constraint the reference class keeps revealing. The risk: the highest uncertainty about impact, a recurring cost that is hard to unwind, and the weakest numbers on paper.

perspectives.title: Build research capacity, then decide on tools
perspectives.text: Fund C now ($640,000 in the first year, under the recurring threshold), use part of the remaining budget for one-time improvements that raise usage of the existing lab, and revisit the platform next year with the club’s own evidence. This treats waiting as an option: the cost is a year of the platform’s benefits; the gain is a better tool decision and a capability whose value the five-year horizon understates. The risk: C has the worst low case of any option and benefits that will be hard to demonstrate quickly to an owner who wants results.

perspectives.title: Argue for the complementary pair
perspectives.text: If the analysis shows that tools and people are complements, splitting the money across substitutes is the worst outcome. Recommend C plus two coaches, accept the wait for ownership approval of a roughly $910,000 recurring commitment, and make the case that the threshold should not decide strategy. The risk: the hiring window may close, ownership may refuse, and the department will have spent its credibility on process rather than results.

case.application: The same structure appears whenever a team must choose among more people, better tools and deeper capability with a fixed budget. Consider the engineering organization of a software company deciding between hiring site-reliability engineers, buying an observability platform with an impressive vendor payback, or forming a small applied-research group. The questions transfer directly: what does the organization’s own record say about adoption of past tools; are people and tools complements, so that funding one without the other repeats past failures; which costs are sunk (the monitoring system bought two years ago); can the purchase be staged with usage milestones; and does a five-year horizon at one discount rate quietly favor the option with fast, visible returns over the one that builds lasting capability?

quiz.title: Week 10 quiz: Finance for executive decision-making

questions.prompt: Halvard Medical Supply (fictional) has grown quickly. Its board is pleased with rising profit, but the treasurer warns that the company will need a credit line within a year. Based on the data, what is the most likely explanation, and what should the board ask first?

stimulus.caption: Halvard Medical Supply, selected figures ($ millions)

options.text: The company is not really profitable; the net income figures are probably misstated.
Growth is absorbing cash in working capital: receivables and inventory are rising far faster than revenue. Ask why customers are paying more slowly and why inventory is building.
Depreciation is rising, which is draining operating cash.
Capital spending on equipment is what turned operating cash flow negative.
The company should cut prices to accelerate sales and restore cash flow.

questions.explanation: Year 3 reconciles exactly: 5.6 + 1.0 − 6.5 (increase in receivables) − 4.5 (increase in inventory) + 3.5 (increase in payables) = −0.9. Receivables rose from about 55 days of revenue (6.0 ÷ 40.0 × 365) to about 91 days (17.0 ÷ 68.0 × 365), so collections are slowing as well as growing. The first questions concern credit terms, collection and inventory policy, not profitability.

optionFeedback.a: Nothing in the data suggests misstated profit; the gap between profit and cash is fully explained by working capital.
optionFeedback.c: Depreciation is a non-cash expense; it is added back in operating cash flow and does not drain cash.
optionFeedback.d: Capital spending appears in investing activities, not in cash from operations.
optionFeedback.e: Faster sales growth on the same terms would absorb even more working capital; price cuts also lower margins.

questions.prompt: Identify the main flaw in this reasoning.

stimulus.text: Fictional memo from a chief executive to a board: “Our EBITDA grew 25% this year, to a record $18 million. That means we are generating more cash than ever, so we can comfortably fund the $15 million expansion from operations next year without borrowing.”

options.text: EBITDA excludes interest and taxes, so the true figure must be higher.
EBITDA ignores capital spending and changes in working capital, both of which consume cash; it is not the cash available to fund an expansion.
A 25% increase cannot be sustained, so the forecast is wrong.
Expansions should always be financed with debt, never from operations.

questions.explanation: EBITDA approximates operating earnings before non-cash charges, but cash available for new investment is closer to operating cash flow minus maintenance capital spending. Growth that ties up receivables and inventory, plus existing capex needs, can leave far less than $18 million — or none — to fund the expansion.

optionFeedback.a: Interest and taxes are real cash outflows; excluding them makes EBITDA higher than cash available, not lower.
optionFeedback.c: Sustainability of growth is a separate question; even at a stable level, EBITDA is not free cash.
optionFeedback.d: The financing mix is a separate decision; the flaw is treating EBITDA as available cash.

questions.prompt: A hospital can buy a sterilization unit for $250,000 that will save $80,000 a year (received at each year end) for four years, with no salvage value. At a 10% discount rate, what is the NPV in dollars? Round to the nearest dollar.
questions.explanation: The savings are worth about $253,589 today at 10%, so the NPV is about $3,589 — positive but thin. Simple payback is 3.1 years (250,000 ÷ 80,000), which looks comfortable; the NPV shows how little margin there is once time value is counted, and a small shortfall in savings would turn it negative.

questions.prompt: Your organization evaluates every proposal at a single 11% hurdle rate. Your energy-efficiency retrofit has very predictable savings and a negative NPV at 11%, but a clearly positive NPV at 6%, a rate comparable to what lenders charge for similarly safe projects. The capital committee meets next week. What is your best move?

options.text: Raise the savings estimate until the project clears 11%.
Present NPV at both the hurdle rate and a risk-appropriate rate, explain why the project is safer than the average investment, and propose that the committee consider a lower-risk tier.
Withdraw the proposal; the hurdle rate is the organization’s policy.
Present only the simple payback period, which avoids the discount-rate question.

questions.explanation: A single hurdle rate penalizes safe projects and favors risky ones. The honest response is to make the risk argument explicit, show both valuations and ask for a rate that matches the project’s risk — a request finance offices can accept without abandoning discipline.

optionFeedback.a: Manipulating forecasts to clear a hurdle is strategic misrepresentation; it destroys trust and the committee’s ability to compare projects.
optionFeedback.c: Withdrawing forgoes a value-creating project without challenging a policy that is distorting choices.
optionFeedback.d: Hiding the time-value question behind payback avoids the real issue and is likely to be spotted.

questions.prompt: An environmental project has cash flows of −$100 now, +$230 in one year and −$132 in two years (a site-restoration cost). An analyst reports “an IRR of 10%.” What is the most accurate statement?

options.text: The IRR is 10%, so the project is acceptable at any cost of capital below 10%.
The project has two IRRs, 10% and 20%; its NPV is positive only for discount rates between them, so a single IRR is misleading and NPV at the actual cost of capital should be used.
The project has no IRR because the cash flows sum to a negative number.
IRR cannot be computed for projects with costs in more than one year.

questions.explanation: With two sign changes, the NPV equation −100 + 230/(1 + r) − 132/(1 + r)² = 0 has two roots, r = 10% and r = 20%. NPV is negative below 10% (at 0% it is −$2) and positive between 10% and 20%. The analyst’s single IRR hides this; the decision should rest on NPV at the relevant rate.

optionFeedback.a: This applies the usual IRR rule to a non-conventional project. Below 10% the NPV is actually negative.
optionFeedback.c: The undiscounted sum is −2, but that does not prevent the IRR equation from having roots; here it has two.
optionFeedback.d: IRR can be computed; the problem is that it may not be unique.

questions.prompt: A hospital’s sleep-medicine service reports a loss and the board asks whether to close it. What is the best decision on financial grounds?

stimulus.caption: Sleep-medicine service, annual ($ millions)
rows: Variable costs (staff paid per study, supplies)
Portion of allocated overhead that would disappear if the service closed

options.text: Close it: it loses $0.2 million a year.
Keep it: closing would remove $0.8 million of contribution and only $0.2 million of avoidable overhead, leaving the hospital $0.6 million a year worse off.
Close it, because allocated overhead is a real cost that every service must cover.
Keep it only if revenue can be raised enough to cover the full $1.0 million of overhead.

questions.explanation: The relevant comparison is avoidable revenue and costs. Closing loses $2.0 million of revenue, saves $1.2 million of variable cost and $0.2 million of avoidable overhead: the hospital is $0.6 million worse off. The other $0.8 million of overhead would simply be reallocated to other services — the start of a “death spiral.” Strategic or quality reasons could still justify closing, but not this financial argument.

optionFeedback.a: The reported loss includes $0.8 million of overhead that does not go away; the service makes a positive contribution to it.
optionFeedback.c: Overhead matters in aggregate, but a decision should count only the overhead it changes.
optionFeedback.d: Full-cost coverage is a pricing goal, not the test for whether to keep an activity that covers its avoidable costs.

questions.prompt: A clinic is deciding whether to replace its current ultrasound machine with a new model. Select every cost that is relevant to the decision.

options.text: The $180,000 the clinic paid for the current machine four years ago.
The $25,000 the current machine would fetch if sold now.
Maintenance the current machine would need over the next three years.
The clinic’s allocated share of hospital administration, which is the same either way.
The purchase price of the new machine.
Staff time needed to train on the new machine.

questions.explanation: Relevant costs are future and differ between the options: the resale value forgone by keeping the old machine, its future maintenance, the new machine’s price and the training time it requires. The original purchase price is sunk, and the allocated administration cost is the same under both options.

questions.prompt: A department has $900 thousand to invest. Projects cannot be split. Project X costs 500 and has an NPV of 120; Y costs 400, NPV 110; Z costs 300, NPV 70; W costs 200, NPV 60 (all in $ thousands). What is the maximum total NPV the department can achieve, in $ thousands?
questions.working: Check feasible combinations within 900: X + Y = 900 → 230; X + Z = 800 → 190; X + W = 700 → 180; Y + Z + W = 900 → 240; Y + Z = 700 → 180; Y + W = 600 → 170; Z + W = 500 → 130. X + Z + W = 1,000 and X + Y + any other exceed the budget. Maximum = 240 (Y + Z + W).
questions.explanation: Picking the largest NPVs first (X then Y) spends the budget for 230; the three smaller projects together deliver 240. With a binding budget and indivisible projects, enumerate the feasible combinations — here ranking by NPV per dollar (W 0.30, Y 0.275, X 0.24, Z 0.233) and then filling remaining room also reaches 240, but neither shortcut is guaranteed in general.

questions.prompt: A city IT department estimates that a new permitting system will cost $2.0 million. An analyst compiles the record of comparable past projects. If leadership wants a budget it has about an 80% chance of staying within, which figure does the reference class support?

stimulus.caption: Reference class: 14 comparable public-sector system replacements (fictional)
stimulus.note: Synthetic data. Ratios above 1.0 indicate overruns.

options.text: $2.0 million — the estimate reflects this project’s own detailed plan.
$2.5 million — the median outcome of the reference class.
$3.2 million — the 80th percentile ratio of 1.60 applied to the estimate.
$2.2 million — the estimate plus a standard 10% contingency.
No budget can be derived because every software project is unique.

questions.explanation: Reference-class forecasting positions the project within the distribution of comparable outcomes. An 80% confidence budget corresponds to the 80th percentile of the overrun distribution: $2.0 million × 1.60 = $3.2 million. The median ($2.5 million) gives only about even odds. Leadership can then decide whether to fund that level, cut scope, or stage the project — and should record why, if at all, this project differs from the class.

optionFeedback.a: This is the inside view; in the reference class, at least three quarters of projects exceeded their approved estimate (the 25th percentile ratio is 1.08).
optionFeedback.b: The median gives roughly a 50% chance of staying within budget, not 80%.
optionFeedback.d: A 10% contingency (a ratio of 1.10) is barely above the class’s 25th percentile, so most comparable projects exceeded it; it falls far short of the 1.60 needed for about 80% confidence.
optionFeedback.e: Uniqueness is the classic inside-view objection; comparable projects still carry information about cost growth.

questions.prompt: A health system is considering a $1.2 million remote patient-monitoring program. The team estimates an expected NPV of about +$250,000, with a 30% chance of losing about $760,000 and a 20% chance of gaining about $1.7 million. The system could absorb the loss. A one-year, two-site pilot costing $100,000 would reveal adoption and reimbursement. Rank these responses from best to worst.

options.text: Fund the pilot with predefined adoption and reimbursement milestones and a written stop rule; decide on full rollout after a year.
Approve the full rollout now: expected NPV is positive and the downside is affordable.
Approve the full rollout only if NPV stays positive after adding five percentage points to the discount rate “for safety.”
Reject the program: a 30% chance of losing $760,000 is unacceptable.

questions.explanation: The pilot buys information that resolves the main uncertainty and avoids most of the downside, at modest cost — the real-option logic. Full approval is defensible because expected value is positive and the loss is absorbable, but it forgoes the option. An arbitrary five-point rate penalty replaces analysis with a rule of thumb and may approve or reject for the wrong reasons. Outright rejection discards positive expected value and the chance to learn cheaply.

questions.prompt: Read the fictional study summary. Which interpretation is best supported?

stimulus.text: Fictional study: Researchers analyzed a professional league from 2010 to 2018. They estimated each skill’s contribution to team wins and the salary premium the market paid for it. A widely read public analysis arguing that “contact skill is underpaid” appeared before the 2015 season.

stimulus.caption: Estimated effects per one-standard-deviation increase in a skill (fictional)
stimulus.note: Synthetic data. Standard errors omitted for brevity.

options.text: Contact skill caused more wins after 2015 because teams paid more for it.

Before 2015 contact skill was priced below its contribution to winning relative to power; the gap narrowed afterward, consistent with an edge that eroded once the insight spread — though the timing alone cannot prove the publication caused the change.
Power skill was overpaid throughout, so teams should stop paying for power.
Because both skills add the same wins, the salary differences must reflect measurement error.

questions.explanation: Equal win contributions with unequal pay indicate relative mispricing of contact skill before 2015; the premium rising toward that of power afterward fits the pattern documented for on-base ability by Hakes and Sauer. But this is an observational before-and-after comparison: other changes around 2015 could explain the shift, so causal language about the publication is not warranted.

optionFeedback.a: The wins contribution is estimated as the same before and after; salaries changed, not productivity.
optionFeedback.c: Power’s premium matched contact’s after 2015; the data show contact was underpriced earlier, not that power is overpaid.
optionFeedback.d: Measurement error is possible, but a systematic shift after a known event is more consistent with repricing.

questions.prompt: In 150–200 words, advise a general manager whether to fund a $1.5 million player development program using the logic of the Lesson 5 worked example (surplus value, break-even uplift). State the objective the decision serves, the two assumptions that drive the result, the break-even condition, and the leading indicators you would agree in advance to decide whether to continue.
questions.modelAnswer: Recommendation: fund the program for one season as a staged commitment, with continuation tied to pre-agreed indicators. Objective: increase the club’s long-run supply of cost-controlled, major-league-quality players — a surplus objective, not this season’s wins. On the example’s assumptions (a $5 million market value per win, $1 million salary per controlled season, three controlled seasons starting five years out), each year of spending breaks even if it produces about 0.09 additional two-win players; at the assumed 0.3 the NPV is about $3.6 million at 8%. Two assumptions drive this: the uplift and the value of a win. Neither can be verified from outcomes within the decision horizon, because player outcomes are noisy and lagged. So the case rests on mechanism and intermediate evidence. Before funding, agree on leading indicators — for example, targeted skill metrics in the participating cohort versus a comparison cohort, availability and durability, and staff adoption — with thresholds that trigger expansion, revision or stopping after one season. Record the decision and forecast in the decision journal.

levels: 1 — recommendation without an explicit objective (or vice versa)
2 — explicit objective and a clear, conditional recommendation

rubric.criterion: Correct use of surplus value and break-even logic
levels: 0 — no quantitative reasoning or wrong logic
1 — mentions NPV or break-even without correct use
2 — correct break-even or NPV logic with minor errors
3 — correct surplus, NPV and break-even reasoning tied to the decision

rubric.criterion: Identifies the driving assumptions and their measurability
levels: 1 — names assumptions but not why they are hard to verify
2 — names uplift and win value and explains why outcomes cannot confirm them soon

rubric.criterion: Pre-agreed leading indicators and decision triggers
levels: 2 — specific indicators but no stop/expand rule
3 — specific indicators, comparison, thresholds and a stop/expand rule

reserve.prompt: A company begins the year with retained earnings of $10.0 million, earns net income of $3.0 million and pays $1.0 million in dividends. What are its retained earnings at year end, in $ millions?
reserve.working: Ending retained earnings = beginning retained earnings + net income − dividends = 10.0 + 3.0 − 1.0 = 12.0.
reserve.explanation: Net income links the income statement to the balance sheet through retained earnings; distributions to owners reduce them. This is one of the core links among the three statements.

reserve.prompt: A firm is financed 50% by equity costing 10% and 50% by debt costing 6% before tax. Its tax rate is 21%. What is its weighted average cost of capital, in percent?
reserve.explanation: WACC weights each source of capital by its share and uses the after-tax cost of debt because interest is tax-deductible. It is the right discount rate only for projects whose risk resembles the firm’s average.

reserve.prompt: A senior analyst spends twelve hours a week producing a manual report that two executives skim. Her salary is fixed. What is the most accurate description of the report’s cost?

options.text: Zero, because her salary is paid regardless.
About 30% of her salary, the share of her week it uses.
The value of the most important work she could do with those twelve hours instead.
The printing and distribution cost of the report.

reserve.explanation: Fixed salaries make staff time feel free, but the economic cost of the report is its opportunity cost: the best alternative use of those hours. That can be far more or far less than a salary share, depending on what she would otherwise do.

optionFeedback.a: This confuses accounting cost with economic cost; scarce hours have alternative uses.
optionFeedback.b: A salary share is an accounting allocation; it does not measure what the hours could produce elsewhere.
optionFeedback.d: Direct costs are trivial here; the main cost is the forgone use of expert time.

reserve.prompt: A critic says a club “overpays” for top draft picks because, on average, those picks deliver less surplus value per dollar of draft capital than later picks. What is the strongest response, drawing on the debate between Massey and Thaler and Brill and Wyner?

options.text: The critic is wrong because surplus value cannot be measured.

Whether this is overpaying depends on the club’s objective: if elite players are disproportionately valuable — for example, for championship chances — paying a premium for a higher chance of landing one can be rational.
Top picks always deliver more surplus in total, so the critic misunderstands the data.
Markets for draft picks are efficient by definition, so no overpayment is possible.

reserve.explanation: Massey and Thaler’s evidence concerns average surplus; Brill and Wyner argue the overvaluation conclusion depends on assuming clubs should maximize expected surplus. With skewed payoffs, other objectives can justify the premium. The right move is to state the objective before judging efficiency.

optionFeedback.a: Surplus value is estimated with error but can be measured; the debate is about the objective, not measurability.
optionFeedback.c: The research found the very top picks yield less surplus on average than later first-round picks.
optionFeedback.d: Market efficiency is an empirical claim, and the evidence suggests these markets can misprice.

assignment.title: The Business Case: Financial Justification for an Investment

brief.text: Write a financial and strategic justification for an investment of your choice: a new department or role, a technology system, a facility, a research program or another organizational initiative. It must be hypothetical and non-confidential. Use invented names and synthetic numbers; do not use any real organization’s budget, salaries or internal data. A good choice is something you could plausibly propose in your field within the next two years, so that the reasoning is worth keeping.

The case is written for a skeptical decision-maker with authority over the money — a president, a chief financial officer or a board committee — who has twenty minutes and will ask what else the money could do. It should let them see the decision, the alternatives, the cash flows and the assumptions behind them, the uncertainty, and what you would treat as evidence of success or failure.

items: Build a simple cash-flow model (a spreadsheet is fine) for at least two real options plus “do nothing” or “status quo.” Show yearly cash flows, not accounting profit.
State and justify the discount rate, and report NPV first, then IRR and payback as context.
Include at least one sensitivity table (one assumption at a time) and low / base / high scenarios with probabilities; report expected NPV and the break-even value of the assumption that matters most.
Apply the outside view: describe a reference class (even an informal one) for your key cost or adoption assumption and adjust for it.
Name the opportunity cost explicitly — the best alternative use of the same money and staff time — and say what the investment displaces.
Describe non-financial value and risks honestly; do not convert everything into dollars, but do not hide behind “strategic value” either.

brief.text: Automated checks confirm only format (word count and that each template section is present). The rubric is for your self-assessment or for a reviewer; APERTURE does not grade the content of your argument automatically.

assignment.deliverable: An 800–1,200-word business case with a one-page cash-flow and sensitivity appendix, recommending whether and how to make a hypothetical investment.

template.heading: Decision and recommendation
template.guidance: In three or four sentences: the decision, your recommendation, its expected NPV and the single condition that would change your mind.

template.heading: Context and options
template.guidance: Why now; the objective the investment serves; at least two real options plus do-nothing, each described in one or two sentences.

template.heading: Cash-flow assumptions
template.guidance: Costs (one-time and recurring, including implementation and staff time) and benefits by year, with the source or reasoning for each. Mark which numbers are estimates and from whom. Note what is sunk and excluded.

template.heading: NPV, IRR and payback
template.guidance: Discount rate and why it fits the project’s risk; NPV for each option; IRR and payback as context; any ranking disagreements and how you resolved them.

template.heading: Sensitivity and scenarios
template.guidance: A one-at-a-time sensitivity table, low / base / high scenarios with probabilities, expected NPV, the break-even value of the key assumption, and the reference-class adjustment.

template.heading: Non-financial value and opportunity cost
template.guidance: Benefits and costs outside the cash flows (mission, capability, relationships, ethics); what the money and staff time would otherwise do; the NPV you are asking the decision-maker to give up for non-financial value, if any.

template.heading: Risks, staging and decision triggers
template.guidance: Main risks and mitigations; how the investment could be staged, piloted or abandoned; the leading indicators and thresholds, agreed in advance, that will trigger expansion, revision or exit.

template.heading: Recommendation and request
template.guidance: Exactly what you are asking for (amount, timing, approvals) and what you will report back, when.

levels.label: Beginning

scenario.text: Draft your business case for a skeptical decision-maker who controls the money and will ask what else it could do. Lead with the recommendation and its expected value, then show how you know.

audience.who: Chief financial officer or finance lead
audience.cares: Cash flows, the discount rate, double-counted benefits, recurring commitments and what happens in the downside.
Fit with the organization’s objective, what the investment displaces, and how success or failure will be recognized early.

audience.who: The staff who will carry it out
audience.cares: Workload, whether the tools or roles will actually be used, and whether the plan is realistic.

checklist: Recommendation and expected NPV in the first two sentences
At least two options plus do-nothing, compared on the same basis
Cash flows by year, not accounting profit; sunk costs excluded
Discount rate stated and justified for this project’s risk
Break-even value of the key assumption reported
Reference class named for the main cost or adoption assumption
Displaced alternative and its value named explicitly
Pre-agreed indicators and thresholds for expand, revise or stop

prompts: Recall a budget or investment decision you influenced. Which number carried the argument — profit, cash, NPV, payback or an average cost — and was it the right one for the question?
Name one sunk cost you or your organization is still defending. What would you decide if you were arriving fresh today, and what makes that hard to say aloud?
Where in your current work is staff time treated as free? What is the most valuable thing that time could be doing instead?
Think of a proposal you expect to make in the next year. What reference class would a skeptical finance partner use to challenge your forecast, and what does it say?

review.front: Why can a fast-growing company report rising profit while its operating cash flow falls?
review.back: Accrual profit counts revenue when earned; growth ties up cash in receivables and inventory (working capital), so cash lags profit.

review.front: Operating cash flow by the indirect method starts from net income and then…?
review.back: Adds non-cash expenses (depreciation), subtracts increases in receivables and inventory, and adds increases in payables.

review.front: How does buying equipment for cash appear in the first year’s statements?
review.back: Full payment as an investing outflow; only one year of depreciation as expense; the asset, net of depreciation, on the balance sheet.

review.front: What does the discount rate represent in an NPV calculation?
review.back: The opportunity cost of capital: the return available on alternative investments of similar risk.

review.front: Two mutually exclusive projects: one has the higher IRR, the other the higher NPV at the cost of capital. Which do you choose?
review.back: The higher NPV at the appropriate rate (or compare the IRR of the incremental cash flows with the cost of capital).
WACC = (E/V) × cost of equity + (D/V) × cost of debt × (1 − tax rate).

review.front: What is the present value of $1,000 received in three years at 8%?

review.back: Fixed costs ÷ contribution margin per unit (price − variable cost per unit).

review.front: Which costs belong in a decision?
review.back: Only future costs that differ between the options (incremental, avoidable); sunk costs count only through salvage or reuse value.

review.front: Why can ranking by profitability index fail under capital rationing?
review.back: With indivisible projects, a ranking can strand budget; the best set must be found by checking feasible combinations.

review.front: What did Frederick and colleagues find about opportunity costs?
review.back: People often neglect them; simple cues naming the alternative use of money reduced purchases, and effort alone did not overcome the neglect.

review.front: Why is expected NPV often lower than the base-case NPV?
review.back: Base cases usually describe the plan working; when downside scenarios are larger than upside ones, the probability-weighted average falls below the base.

review.front: Three conditions for a real option to be valuable?
review.back: Uncertainty that will actually resolve, an investment that is costly to reverse, and willingness to act on what is learned — including stopping.

review.front: The three steps of reference-class forecasting?
review.back: Identify comparable past projects; establish the distribution of their outcomes; position the new project in it and adjust only for documented differences.

review.front: Why can an expensive club be spending rationally despite a poor cost per marginal win?
review.back: Win value is nonlinear: wins near a postseason threshold can be worth far more than average, so marginal value can justify a high marginal cost.

review.front: What is the core of the dispute between Massey and Thaler and Brill and Wyner?
review.back: Whether top draft picks are overpriced depends on the objective: expected surplus says yes; valuing the chance of an elite player can make the premium rational.
